58.titleEn: Sizing a Large Gear Heat Treatment Furnace: Freeze Six Boundaries Before Dimensions
58.summaryEn: Work from workpiece and fixture envelopes through heat circulation, the effective zone, handling and site clearances.
58.contentEn:
Do not size a large-gear heat treatment furnace by adding a fixed margin to the largest part. Freeze the workpiece envelope and load, then check fixture space, required circulation, effective zone, handling and site movements on one layout before deciding equipment dimensions.

Suneng box-furnace documents distinguish the effective furnace zone from the basket's usable loading dimensions; internal loading space is not the basket's outside envelope. A large-gear project likewise needs the gear outline, loading orientation and complete tooling envelope, compared with the proposed working zone and handling passages. If chamber dimensions are based only on gear diameter, complete the loaded arrangement before freezing dimensions. Do not borrow clearance values from another workpiece.

Suneng's engineering team uses six checks: workpiece envelope, loading task, fixture space, heat-circulation requirements, effective working zone and movement/site verification. They apply to trolley length, width and height as well as pit diameter, depth and building clearance. Choose the arrangement for the workpiece orientation and process.

Physical fit is not the complete sizing task

A part that fits statically may still lie outside the agreed effective zone or prevent loading, circulation, transfer or maintenance. Define chamber geometry and the effective working zone separately, linking the latter to the test region, state and criteria. Workpieces, fixtures, supports and required spacing must be checked together. No universal clearance replaces that design review.

Six steps to freeze dimensions

1. List workpiece envelopes

Supply material, diameter, thickness/height and weight for maximum and usual specifications. The largest item defines the capability boundary, while common products define routine combinations. Enlarging only for the largest item can leave an impractical everyday loading arrangement.

2. Draw the loading task

Flat, layered and approved vertical arrangements require different width, height, diameter, depth and lifting space. Single, same-size and mixed batches also differ. A trolley route requires horizontal loading, capacity, door and travel checks. A pit route requires vertical fixtures, depth, lifting gear, building height and foundations. These differences inform dimensions, not universal superiority.

3. Include fixtures

Blocks, trays, supports and dedicated fixtures occupy space and participate in loading, lifting and transfer. Define their dimensions, support locations, hot-use arrangement and relationship to the workpiece before freezing size. A support arrangement is not a distortion guarantee without process and structural verification.

4. Check heat circulation

Large gears and fixtures change flow and heat exchange. Confirm workpiece-to-workpiece and workpiece-to-boundary space from loading, circulation and equipment design rather than a fixed allowance.

5. Freeze the effective working zone

Check the complete loaded arrangement to confirm that the parts requiring heat treatment lie within the agreed effective zone, while checking tooling, supports, required spacing and handling passages together. Structure, insulation, heating/circulation, door/lid and trolley/body design then establish geometric equipment dimensions. Acceptance returns to the agreed zone, state and method.

6. Verify movements and site conditions

Check full door/lid opening, trolley or lifting travel, building obstructions, exit and quench-transfer paths and component removal for maintenance. Trolley proposals typically need rails, front clearance, foundations and crane coverage; pit proposals need foundations, height, vertical lifting, lid movement and protection.

Documents to confirm for an enquiry

  • Maximum/usual workpiece dimensions, individual weights and materials.
  • Quantity, combinations and orientation.
  • Fixtures, supports, lifting gear and combined drawings.
  • Written and drawn effective-zone definition.
  • Equipment envelope and door, lid, trolley or lifting movement envelopes.
  • Exit, transfer, quench and maintenance routes.
  • Foundations, height, crane, energy and utility interfaces.
  • Written dimension-freeze and acceptance responsibilities.

These make physical fit, practical handling and testability separate verifiable facts. They do not themselves guarantee hardness, structure or distortion.

Suneng can assess dimensions and proposals from workpieces, process, loading, fixtures, transfer and site data and help define the zone, handling, supply and acceptance. Final type, parameters and deliverables follow the agreed technical documents.

57.titleEn: Temperature Uniformity Acceptance for Gear Quenching and Tempering: Separate Equipment, Workpiece and Product
57.summaryEn: Connect three evidence layers without treating furnace-temperature tests as proof of every workpiece or product result.
57.contentEn:
Suneng's engineering team recommends three linked evidence layers: define how the equipment is tested within an effective zone, temperature and state; define whether and how workpiece temperatures and the actual treatment are recorded; then inspect hardness, microstructure, distortion and other results under the product and process documents.

Suneng box-furnace documents record furnace-control points separately from workpiece-monitoring points. Gear-treatment acceptance can use the same distinction between objects: check the furnace working-zone test, the temperature and process records for the actual gears, and the required hardness, microstructure or other product inspections. Recording arrangements for other workpieces do not determine gear sensor counts or prove gear results.

Empty-furnace deviation is not workpiece-temperature deviation

Empty, agreed-load and production states differ in thermal load, shielding, circulation paths and heat absorption. Use a test conclusion only within its reported state and agreed basis for extension.

Furnace points describe the temperature field at defined positions. Heating within or on a gear also depends on material, dimensions, orientation, fixtures, load combination and heat transfer. An empty-furnace result cannot become a claim that all gears have identical temperature, hardness, structure or distortion.

Layer 1: equipment temperature uniformity

  1. Effective zone: identify the test and guaranteed region in words and drawings.
  2. Temperature: list the temperatures to verify.
  3. State: identify empty, agreed-load or other accepted conditions and the loading details.
  4. Points/instruments: cover the agreed zone using traceable instruments, sensors and recorders.
  5. Stabilisation/records: define start, recording range, data sources and abnormal-event treatment.
  6. Calculation/criteria: define the data, calculation and evaluation, distinguishing different measurement sources.
  7. Report/retest: retain state, region, point map, instruments, raw data, calculations, abnormalities, deviations and retest conclusions.

This article gives no universal tolerance, point count, spacing, stabilisation time or recording period. The agreement, acceptance plan and applicable documents define them.

Layer 2: workpiece temperatures and the treatment process

Consider how gears heat, hold, proceed to quenching and then complete high-temperature tempering and subsequent cooling under the agreed process and actual load. The process owner determines whether workpiece measurements are needed, and their location, recording and criteria, using material, sizes, orientation, fixtures, quantity, circulation and transfer requirements.

Equipment testing assesses the defined furnace zone; workpiece measurement follows specific parts under specific conditions. Door/lid opening, trolley or lifting movement, exit, transfer and entry into quenching also belong in the process evidence. Transfer requirements come from the process documents.

Layer 3: product results

Hardness, microstructure and distortion also depend on initial material, prior processing, heating, holding, transfer, quench cooling, high-temperature tempering and its subsequent cooling, and inspection. Define sample locations, methods, criteria and treatment of nonconformities from the product drawings and process agreement.

The layers must link without substituting for one another: equipment reports establish the tested state, process records establish how that load was handled and treated, and product reports establish whether the inspected products meet their requirements.

Factory/site tests and targets/measurements

Factory testing does not automatically replace site testing after transport, installation, foundations, utilities and loading changes. The agreed documents determine retests, states and criteria.

Keep design targets, contractual guarantees and measured values separate. A target becomes an agreed contractual boundary only with its conditions, method and responsibility defined; a measured value requires the corresponding test and report.

Suneng can support contracted uniformity and control-system accuracy checks and help define testing and records. Qualified organisations perform calibration or third-party certification where required. Actual parameters, tests, responsibility and delivery follow the confirmed documents.

56.titleEn: Quoting a Trolley Furnace for Large Gear Quenching and Tempering: Specify the Workpiece First
56.summaryEn: Prepare eight input groups and four confirmation documents before comparing furnace dimensions, configuration and price.
56.contentEn:
For a large-gear quenching-and-tempering trolley-furnace quotation, provide eight aligned inputs: workpiece envelope, loading duty, treatment curve, quench transfer, energy, controls/traceability, acceptance and site supply. Gear diameter, chamber dimensions or load weight alone cannot define the full scope.

A Suneng variable-capacity trolley-furnace proposal assigns support blocks and tooling to the buyer, with the buyer supplying product geometry and the seller providing the design. A large-gear enquiry should distinguish workpieces, supporting tooling and site rails. If only the furnace is quoted, clarify racks, supports, handling, rails and quenching provisions. A historical proposal explains supply responsibilities; it does not establish the price or load capacity for a different gear-processing duty.

This is an enquiry-preparation method, not a universal price formula. Suneng's engineering team recommends explaining what will be treated, how production will run, how it will be accepted and what the site provides. The equipment supplier can then assess effective zone, loading, thermal design, movements and interfaces. Type, parameters, price and supply follow the agreed documents.

Why chamber dimensions are insufficient

The same furnace name can cover different grades, workpiece ranges, quantities, layouts, fixtures, curves, transfers and utilities. Geometric space is not the effective working zone. Workpieces and fixtures must fit the agreed zone and align with structural loading, heat transfer, movement and temperature-test boundaries. Freeze the production task before defining geometry and price scope.

Eight enquiry inputs

1. Workpiece envelope

Supply material, maximum and usual dimensions, outside diameter, thickness/height, individual weight and drawings or a layout-ready list. The largest part sets the capability boundary; usual parts establish daily combinations. Diameter alone does not describe support, arrangement or handling.

2. Loading task

State quantity, mixed loading, flat or another confirmed orientation, and tray, block, support and lifting-fixture dimensions and weights. Check individual weight, total load, fixture weight and distribution on one loading drawing. Deck size alone is insufficient.

3. Quenching-and-tempering curve

The buyer or process owner supplies material, heating, holding, cooling route and production-cycle requirements. The supplier uses these to assess heating, circulation, controls and movements. One maximum temperature is not a complete curve; agree actual temperatures, times and evaluation in the project documents.

4. Quench transfer

Door opening, trolley travel, lifting/transfer and entry into the cooling medium affect layout and auxiliaries. Specify routes, associated equipment, logistics, safety separation and responsibility points. This article gives no universal transfer time and does not equate successful movement with acceptable product properties.

5. Utilities

State available electricity or gas, connection locations and other services. Energy routes create different heating, distribution, gas, exhaust and safety work. Installed capacity is not actual consumption and cannot alone determine operating cost.

6. Controls and traceability

Define programs, temperatures, alarms, permissions, retention and interlocks, including signals to quenching, lifting or other systems. Brands/models do not replace functions, quantities, interfaces and documents. Additional zones do not automatically improve the temperature field.

7. Acceptance

Movements, controls, effective-zone temperature tests, workpiece temperatures and product inspection are different levels. State what is checked at the factory and site, with region, state, points, instruments, records, criteria and retests. Keep inputs/targets, contractual guarantees and measurements distinct.

8. Site and supply

Assign transport, unloading, lifting, foundations, rails, crane, utilities, cables, exhaust, installation, commissioning, training, spares and documents, including handover locations. “Included,” “supervised” and “customer's responsibility” still need precise scope.

Four confirmation documents before a quotation

  1. Workpiece/loading sheet: largest/usual parts, quantities, orientations, fixtures and distribution.
  2. Process/transfer description: material, curve, cooling route, movements and production organisation.
  3. Site-condition sheet: energy, utilities, foundations, lifting, logistics and space.
  4. Responsibility/acceptance sheet: supply, exclusions, factory/site tests, documents and retests.

Use the same inputs to compare technical deviations and commercial differences. This distinguishes price differences caused by configuration, supply, tests or assumptions.

Common questions

Can diameter and weight support an initial quote?

They can start a discussion, but a comparable formal scope also needs usual parts, loading, fixtures, curves, transfer, utilities, controls, acceptance and site inputs. List gaps and assumptions explicitly.

Is a larger chamber the safer choice?

Not automatically. Size follows workpieces, fixtures, effective zone, heat transfer, structural load and movement envelopes. Unjustified enlargement can change investment, energy, footprint and production without improving temperature or product results.

Does equipment acceptance prove gear hardness and distortion?

No. Material, prior processing, loading, treatment, transfer, cooling and inspection also affect results. Agree and record equipment, workpiece-temperature and product checks separately.

Suneng's engineering and service scope

Suneng designs, manufactures and integrates industrial and heat treatment equipment and provides commissioning, retrofit and support. It can assess large-gear trolley proposals, supply interfaces and acceptance from agreed workpiece, process, loading, transfer, utility and site information.

It does not offer per-piece treatment services or replace the buyer/process owner's responsibility for the product process and quality. Exact parameters, price, tests, installation and support follow the technical proposal, agreement, quotation and contract.

55.titleEn: How to Read Trolley Furnace Specifications: Eight Parameters and Four Evidence States
55.summaryEn: Identify what each parameter measures, its operating conditions and whether it is an input, target, guarantee or measured result.
55.contentEn:
Read eight parameter groups—effective zone, load, temperature/curve, uniformity, heating capability, power/energy, controls/records and actions/interlocks—then label each value as a purchasing input, design target, contract guarantee or measured result. State its object, conditions, stage and verification method before using it for selection or acceptance.

Suneng box-furnace documents distinguish the effective furnace zone from the loading basket's usable internal dimensions. Identify whether a figure describes furnace space, basket interior or workpiece outline. If the answer is only that the load fits, request the basket's outside dimensions, fork-tine passages and actual loading layout. Clear space dimensions do not establish load capacity, movement or process performance.

Suneng's engineering team calls this method “eight parameters, four evidence states.” It identifies missing or mixed information in technical tables. It does not replace the project agreement, applicable requirements, calibration or site tests. Actual values and criteria follow the confirmed documents.

Four states of a parameter

  • Procurement input: buyer-supplied workpiece, process, output, energy and site conditions.
  • Design target: a proposed engineering objective, not an acceptance result.
  • Contractual guarantee: the agreed responsibility in the contract or technical agreement.
  • Measured result: a record obtained for a defined region, state, instrument and method.

These cannot replace each other. A design target is not a measurement, and one measured result cannot be extended to every load and temperature.

1. Effective working zone

Distinguish chamber geometry from the agreed loading and process-verification area. State dimensions, location and drawing reference, aligned with loading and temperature-test regions. Chamber dimensions alone do not establish whether every workpiece and fixture is within the agreed zone or which space a result describes.

2. Loading capability

Identify maximum/usual parts, individual weights, quantities, fixtures, total load, distribution and handling. Equal total weight with different support or distribution can create different structural and movement duties. A deck size or single load figure cannot describe every loading condition.

3. Temperatures and curve

Maximum permissible temperature, usual working temperature, full heating/holding/cooling curve and door/transfer conditions are separate inputs. A maximum alone does not establish process coverage or cycle. Identify the measured object and state, with the required range defined by the process documents.

4. Temperature uniformity

Attach the effective zone, temperature, empty or agreed load, points/instruments, stabilisation/records, calculation/evaluation and retest method. Without these, deviation figures cannot compare proposals. Furnace uniformity is not workpiece temperature and does not itself prove hardness, microstructure or distortion.

5. Heating capability

Heating time or rate needs start/end conditions, measured object, load, curve and allowed control method. Empty, fixture-only and production-loaded heating are different results. Thermal capacity, structure, losses, heat input and controls also affect performance; no universal heating time applies.

6. Power and consumption

Electric installed power describes configuration and the supply requirement. Gas proposals need fuel conditions, combustion capacity, air, exhaust and safeguards. Neither rating directly establishes consumption. Align workpieces, loading, process, output, meters and periods before comparing energy. Higher power or newer components do not prove a saving.

7. Controls and records

Instrument/sensor accuracy, control stability, furnace distribution and workpiece temperature are different subjects. Specify zones, programs, records, alarms, permissions, retention, interfaces and documents rather than only brands or zone count. Match zones to the design, load and control strategy and verify them.

8. Movements and interlocks

For trolley, door, heat source, circulation, quenching and related equipment, state permitted states, triggers, prohibited actions, alarms, abnormal responses and reset conditions. “Interlocked” or “automatic” is insufficient for a test plan. Safety functions require project risks, applicable requirements and site management; equipment configuration does not replace operating and maintenance responsibilities.

How the parameters affect procurement

Common questions

Does a longer specification mean a more complete proposal?

No. Object, conditions, units, state, responsibility and verification matter more than repeated brands and terminology.

Does control accuracy represent uniformity?

No. Control performance, temperature distribution and workpiece measurement need separate definitions and records.

Does higher installed power guarantee faster heating?

54.titleEn: How Should Trolley Furnace Power Be Selected? Higher Power Does Not Mean Lower Energy Use
54.summaryEn: Separate installed heating capacity, operating input and metered energy, then review loading, curves, losses, zones and utilities.
54.contentEn:
Installed power needs a stated equipment boundary. Identify the installed rating of the heating circuits separately from the total installed electrical load of the furnace, including fans, drives and controls. Actual input during a stage depends on the program, power regulation, loading and heat losses. Metered electrical energy belongs to a defined measurement boundary and reporting period. These are three different quantities.

The total line power and rated quench-furnace heating power in Suneng mesh-belt line documents cover different equipment boundaries. Ask what equipment and loads a quoted power figure includes, then check workpieces, tooling, heat-up and soaking duties and operating arrangements. Do not omit auxiliaries when assessing plant supply, or treat rated power multiplied by annual operating hours as an actual electricity-use record.

Freeze workpieces, fixtures and loading first

Specify material, maximum and usual workpieces, individual weight, batch quantity, fixture weight, total load, distribution and initial condition. In the same chamber, different total heat capacities, packing densities or supports can create different duties. Dimensions alone cannot connect power selection to production.

Then freeze the process curve and cycle

Temperature is only part of the input. Define heating, holding, cooling or furnace cooling, permitted heating rate, door/transfer conditions and daily or shift organisation. Rapid heat-up and deliberately slow programmed heating require different capacity and control considerations. Holding mainly replaces continuing losses; heating also supplies energy to workpieces, fixtures and furnace structure. One simple rule cannot represent both.

Separate useful heating tasks from losses

The buyer need not perform the entire heat balance, but should ask whether the proposal includes workpiece and fixture heating, lining and trolley thermal storage, ongoing body losses, door opening and trolley movement, and exhaust or atmosphere exchange. State whether auxiliary electricity is included in the metering boundary. Structure and duty vary, so fixed coefficients cannot produce a universal power rating. A thermal engineer should review the calculations and margin for the project.

Three quantities to keep separate

QuantityWhat it describesProcurement check
Installed power, with its scope statedRated power for the specified equipment scope. Distinguish the heating circuits from the complete furnace, including auxiliaries.Confirm what the rating includes, then match loading, cycle, zones and supply.
Operating inputPower actually applied during a stage.Program, regulation, load and records.
Metered electrical energyMeter readings for the agreed scope and period.Meter points, time, duty and output.

Heating-circuit rating multiplied by hours is a nominal full-rating calculation, not an actual meter record. It also cannot represent total equipment electricity where fans, drives and controls are included. Compare proposals using equivalent workpieces, loads, curves, output, boundaries and periods.

Review power with zones, controls and supply

The same total power can have different element layouts, zones and operating strategies. Explain distribution, regulation, sensing, records and abnormal-state interlocks. More zones do not automatically improve the temperature field; match them to body, loading, circulation, openings and objectives and verify by the agreed method. Check site distribution capacity, incoming cables, switchgear, auxiliary loads and interlocks.

Record the selection basis

Document procurement inputs, heating tasks and loss categories, zone/control approach, contracted capability and test state, loaded commissioning and metering conditions. These establish a traceable decision, not a fixed contract chapter list. The parties must agree what is guaranteed and how it will be tested.

Common questions

Does higher power always mean faster heating?

No. Workpiece and fixture heat capacity, distribution, curve, furnace storage/losses, element layout, circulation and control strategy also matter.

Can higher power increase electricity use?

The rating alone cannot establish energy per batch. Compare actual records for load, program, holding losses, openings, waiting, auxiliaries and the reporting period.

Can power be estimated at quotation stage?

Yes, conditionally, with missing inputs and assumptions stated. A preliminary calculation is not a final configuration or acceptance guarantee and requires engineering review when inputs are complete.

Suneng's scope

Suneng designs, manufactures and integrates industrial and heat treatment equipment and provides commissioning, retrofit and support. It can assess trolley heating power, zones, supply interfaces and acceptance from agreed workpiece, fixture, load, curve, cycle, energy and site inputs.

This guidance does not promise a project power rating, consumption, heating time, uniformity, product quality or saving. Configuration, tests, installation and support follow the agreed proposal, technical and acceptance documents, quotation and contract.

52.titleEn: What Determines Trolley Furnace Energy Consumption? Compare Energy per Tonne, Not Only per Hour
52.summaryEn: Use actual metered energy and conforming output under consistent loading, process and reporting conditions.
52.contentEn:
To assess trolley-furnace energy consumption, match energy records to conforming output from the same reporting period. Check workpieces, fixtures, loading, curves, door/exhaust conditions, shifts and abnormal states. Installed power or one hour of use cannot establish energy per unit of product.

Suneng mesh-belt line documents distinguish total line power from the heating power of an individual furnace. For an energy comparison, state which equipment the electricity or gas meter actually covers and match it to acceptable output over the same period. If only a plant-wide bill is available, identify other equipment, auxiliary systems and non-production consumption. Installed power and metered energy are different quantities.

Align five measurement definitions first

  1. Define the metering boundary: one furnace or a line, and which heating, circulation, drive and control systems are included.
  2. Keep actual energy readings. Installed power multiplied by time does not replace meter data.
  3. Define conforming output for the same period. Energy per tonne, piece, batch and furnace load are different measures.
  4. Attach workpieces, fixtures, load, program, shifts, door opening, exhaust and abnormal states to the data.
  5. Compare only when these conditions match or their differences can be explained.

A high figure identifies a need to investigate, not the cause

At the production level, examine underloading, frequent changeovers, waiting and empty holding. At the equipment and thermal level, examine lining, seals, heat loss, exhaust, circulation and heating. At the controls and measurement level, examine program versions, instruments and changes to metering points. Confirm each possibility with records and inspections.

For different equipment, shifts or before/after retrofit data, align comparable workpieces and fixtures, loading, curves, energy and equipment boundaries, conforming-output definitions, reporting periods and abnormal-event explanations. If they cannot be aligned, mark the comparison as unresolved or not directly comparable.

49.titleEn: Which Furnace Suits Large Gear Quenching and Tempering? Start with Diameter, Weight and Transfer
49.summaryEn: Compare trolley and pit arrangements after fixing six workpiece, loading, process and site conditions.
49.contentEn:
Outside diameter or a furnace name alone cannot determine the equipment for large-gear quenching and tempering. Establish the workpiece envelope, weight and batch, loading orientation, fixture support, full process curve, quench transfer and site conditions before comparing trolley and pit furnaces.

Suneng pit-furnace documents separately describe suspension tooling, supports on either side of the furnace platform and cover movement, including the division of tooling design and fabrication responsibilities. When assessing a vertical gear arrangement, obtain the load-path, space and handling information for those gears and their tooling. A long-shaft suspension example does not prove gear compatibility. Where horizontal loading suits the workpieces and site, compare a trolley arrangement using the same inputs.

The question is how the gear can heat on stable supports, leave the furnace safely and reach quenching within its process requirements. Horizontal complete-batch loading may favour a trolley arrangement where rails, foundations and lifting are available. Vertical support may favour a pit arrangement where clear height, lifting, fixture stability and transfer are feasible. Special atmosphere, vacuum or other requirements need dedicated assessment.

Six conditions for initial selection

Workpiece envelope

Confirm thickness, individual weight, usual sizes, quantity and total load as well as maximum diameter. The largest part defines a capability limit; usual products and batches determine daily utilisation.

Loading orientation

Flat, layered or vertical arrangements change space, lifting, support forces and transfer. Select for the workpiece, process and site rather than habit.

Fixtures and supports

They must meet loading, hot-service, handling and transfer needs. Support locations, fixture weight and occupied space belong in the effective-zone calculation from the start.

Process curve

Specify material, heating, holding, cooling and tempering, process records and product evaluation. Maximum temperature alone cannot define heating, circulation, controls and records.

Quench transfer

Review door/lid opening, trolley or lifting movement, exit, route clearance, entry into quenching and interlocks on one timeline. The process documents define transfer requirements; there is no universal time for all large gears.

Site

Trolley options need rails, foundations, front clearance and crane coverage. Pit options need foundations/pit, building height, vertical lifting, protection and access. Both need utilities, separated logistics and maintenance space.

Comparing trolley and pit arrangements

Where gear and fixture suit horizontal placement and complete-batch handling, assess trolley loading, effective zone, circulation, seals, transfer and interlocks. Where vertical holding is appropriate, verify fixture stability, clear height, crane lift, entry/exit and transfer before considering a pit furnace.

A pit arrangement does not inherently guarantee lower distortion; the process, fixture and inspection evidence must support that conclusion. Chamber geometry is not the effective zone. Workpieces, fixtures, spacing and heat-transfer requirements determine the usable region, so this article gives no fixed allowance or universal dimension formula.

Separate equipment, process and product acceptance

  • Equipment: effective zone, temperatures/state, points/instruments, stability/records, calculation/criteria, report and retest.
  • Process: loading, fixtures, workpiece temperatures, exit and quench-transfer records.
  • Product: the buyer's material, hardness, microstructure, distortion and inspection requirements.

Furnace uniformity, workpiece temperature consistency and final properties are different subjects. Assign methods and responsibilities separately.

Enquiry checklist

  • Grade, maximum/usual diameter, thickness and individual weight.
  • Quantity, batches, shifts and target cycle.
  • Orientation, fixtures and lifting.
  • Complete treatment and recording requirements.
  • Quench medium, facility, transfer requirement and safety interfaces.
  • Layout, height, crane, foundations, logistics and utilities.
  • Equipment, process and product acceptance.

Suneng can assess trolley or pit proposals and help define the zone, loading, transfer, records, supply and acceptance. Final type, parameters and deliverables follow the agreed technical documents.

48.titleEn: Heat or Flames Leaking at a Trolley Furnace Door? Check Seals, Compression and Furnace Pressure
48.summaryEn: Control the immediate risk, then diagnose the door interface, mechanisms, geometry, pressure, lining and operating state together.
48.contentEn:
Light, escaping hot gas or visible flames around a trolley-furnace door do not automatically mean that replacing the seal will solve the problem. First follow site safety procedures, then examine sealing, compression, distortion, pressure and exhaust, adjacent lining and the closing/loading state as one diagnostic chain.

Suneng gas-fired trolley-furnace documents distinguish the raised-door lock, door-perimeter compression seal and trolley-side seals. Preserve records of actual position, compression movement and contact-surface observations separately. A door-closed signal cannot rule out a sealing or mechanical problem. Use existing records or inspections permitted by site safety conditions; do not approach an active flame leak to take photographs or measurements.

Suneng's engineering team checks whether the surfaces can meet correctly and whether pressure remains within the design condition, together with mechanisms, structure and lining. Closing a visible gap may reduce the symptom without resolving its cause.

Control risk before investigating

Persistent or spreading flames, abnormal pressure or combustion/interlock alarms require the equipment and site's prescribed response, not closer observation or continued faulty operation. Authorised qualified personnel should assess combustion, gas, exhaust and pressure. This article is a diagnostic framework, not an operating procedure, risk analysis or repair instruction.

Six possible causes

1. Seal material or interface failure

Ageing, shrinkage, damage, contamination or a break in the sealing path can allow leakage. Check continuous contact and correct positioning as well as the material's appearance.

2. Incomplete door compression

A sound seal is ineffective if travel is insufficient, forces are uneven, a mechanism sticks or the door fails to reach its design position. More compression is not a universal cure; excessive force can damage seals or mechanisms.

3. Distorted or shifted door, frame or guides

Thermal cycling, impact and changes in foundations or guides can alter alignment. New seal material does not correct the geometry.

4. Pressure or exhaust outside the design condition

Excess positive pressure can force hot gas through weak joints; abnormal negative pressure can draw in cold air and affect temperature and combustion. Review pressure, firing, air and exhaust trends together on gas-fired equipment.

5. Adjacent lining or structural damage

Shrinkage, local damage, thermal bridges or anchor problems can create hot areas resembling seal leakage. Inspect surrounding lining and supports rather than infer a seal-only fault from temperature.

6. Incorrect closing or loading state

An incompletely positioned trolley, debris, obstructing fixtures/load or an incorrect closing sequence can leave the door apparently shut but not seated. Restore the prescribed operating state before deciding that hardware has failed.

A four-step diagnostic sequence

  1. Record the symptom: identify heating, holding or cooling phase and top, side, bottom or multiple locations, with alarms, pressure and combustion records.
  2. Inspect cold: after shutdown and authorised maintenance conditions, examine seals, surfaces, frame, guides, compression, trolley position and adjacent lining.
  3. Assess hot behaviour under authorised conditions: qualified personnel compare joint-temperature distribution, flame location, pressure and combustion/exhaust trends. Images and visual observations are clues, not a complete root-cause conclusion.
  4. Retest after repair: confirm closure/compression, operating pressure, relevant alarms and necessary temperature records, not merely disappearance of visible flame. Retain the results.

Selecting the repair level

If structure and lining are sound, pressure is within the agreed condition and the symptom remains local, investigate the contact surface, seal or compression first. Multiple contact errors or shifted frames/guides require structural or mechanism correction before resealing. Symptoms that track firing, exhaust or pressure require those systems in the diagnosis. Adjacent lining damage may need coordinated seal and lining work. Incorrect positioning or closing requires restoration of the proper state before hardware conclusions.

No universal numerical limit applies to every furnace. Type, heat source, design pressure, sealing arrangement, temperature and technical documents define the boundary.

Information to prepare

Provide type and heat source, operating temperature, leak location and phase, pressure/alarms, seal and compression arrangement, recent repairs and clear cold/hot images obtained only under safe conditions.

Suneng can participate in a combined assessment of doors, seals, lining and pressure systems using equipment records and actual condition. The site inspection, risk review and technical agreement determine repair scope and acceptance.

47.titleEn: How to Read a Trolley Furnace Quotation: Nine Procurement Checks
47.summaryEn: Establish one operating baseline, align nine scope areas and close documented deviations before comparing total prices.
47.contentEn:
Begin with a common workpiece, load, process, output, energy, controls, acceptance and site baseline. Then align nine quotation areas: body, lining, heat source, circulation, controls, trolley, installation, acceptance and commercial terms. Totals are meaningful only when inputs, functions and responsibilities match.

A Suneng gas-fired trolley-furnace quotation presents a summary and itemised breakdown. First align names, quantities, specifications and inclusions within the same version, then check unit prices and totals. Ask the supplier to explain inconsistent scopes or totals in writing and identify the effective version. If the explanation is only that the price has fallen, request an item-by-item difference list; matching names do not establish identical configuration and responsibility.

Suneng's engineering team describes this as one baseline, nine boundaries and documented deviation closure. It is a procurement method, not a compulsory contract structure or a replacement for technical, commercial and contract review.

Establish a comparable baseline

Confirm material, maximum/usual dimensions and individual weight; batch quantity, total load, fixtures and layout; temperature range, complete curve, cooling and surface requirements; complete cycle, shifts, changeovers and output; available power or gas and interfaces; programs, records, alarms, permissions and interlocks; effective zone, test state, method and criteria; and new/retrofit scope, layout, access, foundations and utilities. Put differences in a technical-deviation table instead of reducing everything to one price difference.

1. Body and effective working zone

Compare the effective zone, temperature range, door and loading method, maintenance access and site layout. Geometric chamber dimensions do not automatically describe usable space. Workpieces, fixtures, clearances and circulation determine the relevant area; identical outer or chamber dimensions can conceal different loading conditions.

2. Lining

Compare maximum/usual temperatures, heating and holding, trolley-deck loading, doors, seals and maintenance. Labels such as “all-fibre” or “composite” do not establish identical layers, thickness, anchors, deck refractory or service-life boundaries. Project thermal and structural design determines the materials and structure.

3. Heating or combustion

For electric versions, align circuits, zones and site distribution. For gas versions, align fuel conditions, combustion, air, exhaust and specialist safeguards. Installed power or rated combustion input is not measured consumption or proof of heating and uniformity.

When heat sources differ, first check whether both suit the process/output, then include distribution, gas connections, exhaust and safety in the same scope. Applicable regulations and project documents govern gas safety; this article does not determine compliance.

4. Circulation

Fans, guides and zones do not automatically establish uniformity, and fan checks do not apply to equipment without circulation. Check workpiece, loading, temperature, circulation and test method as one thermal design. Results still require a defined zone, points, state, stabilisation and evaluation.

5. Controls

Compare program operation, temperature records, alarms, permissions, data retention and interlocks between doors, trolley, heating/combustion and associated equipment. Brands and models matter but do not replace functions, quantities, interfaces and documents. Zone count must fit the thermal design and load and be verified by the agreed tests.

6. Trolley

Assess individual and total loads, distribution, fixture weight, rails and handling route together. Deck dimensions alone do not establish load capacity, movement or site logistics. Define foundations, rails, pits, cranes and material-flow responsibility with the installation scope.

7. Installation

Assign connection locations and responsibility for transport, unloading, lifting, foundations, rails, secondary cables, trays, earthing, utilities, exhaust, installation, commissioning and training. “Installation included” and “installation supervision” are different scopes. Customer utilities also need capacity, connection, completion time and cooperation requirements. The contract governs the final responsibility allocation.

8. Acceptance and documents

For uniformity, heating, movement, interlocks, records and loaded trials, specify region, temperature, state, points, instruments, stabilisation, recording, evaluation and retest. Separate targets, guarantees and measured values and distinguish factory and site tests. A proposal target or factory record is not a site measurement.

List drawings, manuals, conformity and test records, together with training scope, format and timing, according to the project.

9. Taxes, transport and commercial terms

Align tax, freight, packaging, insurance, quotation validity, payments, warranty and support. This article supplies no universal commercial terms or historical quotation prices. List commercial differences separately from equipment differences.

Nine-item comparison table

ItemMain checkCommon mistake
BodyZone, temperature, structure and maintenance.Outer dimensions only.
LiningDuty, layers, deck and repair.Material name only.
HeatingEnergy, zones, interfaces and safety.Rated input treated as actual performance.
CirculationApplicable duty, guides, load and tests.A fan treated as proof of uniformity.
ControlsPrograms, records, alarms, permissions and interlocks.Brands or zone count only.
TrolleyLoad, distribution, fixtures, rails and handling.Deck size only.
InstallationTransport, lifting, foundations, utilities and commissioning.No responsibility points.
AcceptanceRegion, state, instruments, method, criteria and retests.Targets presented as measurements.
CommercialTaxes, packing/freight, validity and service.Totals with different boundaries compared directly.

Close deviations explicitly

List substitutions, open items, assumptions and exclusions with impact, owner, confirmer, version and closure evidence. Show unresolved differences separately; do not assume the quotations are equivalent. This process does not replace contractual, claim or legal procedures.

46.titleEn: How Is Trolley Furnace Temperature Uniformity Tested? Define Seven Conditions First
46.summaryEn: Make the zone, temperature, load, instruments, recording, calculations and retests explicit before comparing results.
46.contentEn:
A uniformity test is not a single sensor reading inside a furnace. It is a repeatable survey of the agreed effective zone, temperature and equipment state using traceable instruments and defined point placement, stabilisation, recording, calculation and evaluation.

A Suneng variable-capacity trolley-furnace proposal lists furnace-temperature points separately from workpiece-temperature points. A uniformity test still needs defined test sensors, working zone and loading condition; an existing control or workpiece curve cannot simply be renamed a uniformity report. Match each point on the sensor layout to its channel and original data, then check the temperatures, space and operating state actually covered.

Suneng's engineering team recommends documenting seven conditions before testing. Point counts, positions, durations and tolerances must follow the actual technical agreement, acceptance plan and applicable standards; this article does not supply universal values.

1. Effective working zone: where is the test?

Define the region in text and drawings, including dimensions, position, coordinate reference and boundary. Geometric chamber space is not automatically the effective working zone. Points outside that zone, or tests using different zones, cannot be compared simply through a temperature-deviation number.

2. Test temperatures

A result belongs to its test temperature. Heat balance can differ at other temperatures and control stages. State the temperatures, sequence and whether heating transients are evaluated. Keep design targets, contractual guarantees and measured results separate.

3. Empty, loaded and production states

Loaded tests also depend on workpieces, fixtures, total load, arrangement and heat-transfer obstruction. Use a result only within its tested state and the agreed basis for any extension. Define real workpieces, equivalent load or special fixtures and who approves the layout. An empty test does not establish every loading pattern or replace workpiece-temperature or product-quality inspection.

4. Points and instruments

Points must cover the agreed zone and relevant positions. Their number and arrangement depend on zone, structure, task, agreement, plan and standards. Check the point map and traceable condition of instruments, sensors and recording systems.

Suneng can support contracted uniformity and control-system accuracy checks. Test instruments and sensors need valid verification or calibration records meeting the applicable requirements, including the corrections used for this survey. If third-party certification is required, verify the organisation’s competence and certification scope.

5. Stabilisation and records

State when the agreed stable condition is reached, when recording starts, its duration, the raw data used and handling of stoppages, door openings, sensor problems or other deviations. Implement the applicable standard’s acquisition start, interval, duration or count, and sensor-failure rules. Use continuous traceable records rather than one control-screen image. Distinguish furnace-control readings from independent measurement data.

6. Calculations and evaluation

When using GB/T 9452-2023, correct valid readings for the sensor, compensation cable and instrument, then determine maximum and minimum deviations of actual temperatures from each test setpoint and compare them with the process limits. Highest-minus-lowest temperature is a spread, not a substitute for this evaluation. Define points, acquisition period and abnormal-data handling before testing, while meeting the standard’s test-validity requirements. Changing the interval after seeing results can produce inconsistent conclusions from the same data.

Reference the agreed documents and applicable standards. Record deviation location, possible impact, corrective action, owner and retest method. Verbal explanations do not replace closure evidence.

7. Report and retest

The report should allow another reviewer to reconstruct equipment and test state, zone, temperatures, load, point map, instruments, raw records, calculations, criteria, abnormalities, corrective work and retest conclusions. The contract may add information or adjust the format while retaining the original records and report items required by the applicable standard.

Factory testing does not automatically complete site testing. After transport, installation and utility connections, check the applicable standard’s triggers for a new survey and document the site-test state and method. An agreement alone cannot waive a survey required by that standard.

TemperatureTest points and sequence.Do not extend to every operating temperature.
StateEmpty, agreed load or production.One state does not cover every load.

Stability/recordsConditions, duration and abnormal-data rules.No single-screen conclusions.

Does uniformity establish product quality?

No. Furnace distribution is one equipment check. Workpiece temperature, hardness, structure and distortion also depend on material, prior processing, loading, fixtures, transfer, cooling and inspection. Record equipment results, workpiece temperatures and product inspections separately, with clear responsibilities.

45.titleEn: Electric or Gas-fired Trolley Furnace? Compare Seven Conditions First
45.summaryEn: Align utilities, process, controls, emissions, safety, maintenance and life-cycle costs before choosing the heat source.
45.contentEn:
Neither electric nor gas heating is universally better for a trolley furnace. Energy prices alone are insufficient. Suneng's engineering team first checks whether the site can support each option, then compares the same workpieces, loading, curve and cycle across seven areas.

Suneng curing-furnace documents distinguish combustion flue gas, circulating furnace air and process exhaust. When comparing electric and gas heating, identify not only the heat source but also gases released by the workpieces or process media, how they leave the furnace and who supplies the external system. No combustion flue gas from an electric heat source does not mean that process ventilation or extraction can be omitted.

1. Energy availability

Electric heating needs sufficient electrical and distribution capacity. Gas heating needs pressure, flow, combustion air and exhaust arrangements. Having a connection does not establish the simultaneous capacity needed to operate the equipment.

2. Temperature field and heating

The energy-source name does not determine uniformity or heating rate. Effective zone, loading, element or burner layout, zones, circulation, lining, seals and test methods matter. Define load, points, instruments, test temperature, stabilisation and evaluation with each performance target.

3. Control and regulation

Review electric heating circuits and zone control, or gas pressure, flow and combustion air. Both need the overtemperature, door and movement interlocks appropriate to the project. More zones do not automatically produce a better temperature field.

4. Environmental and exhaust requirements

Resistance heating itself generates no fuel-combustion flue gas. Workpieces, coatings or process media may still generate gases and require ventilation or exhaust. Confirm these separately for the actual duty. Gas-fired options also need combustion and flue-gas boundaries. Environmental, emission and permit conclusions depend on location, the energy system and applicable documents; they cannot be inferred from the heat source alone.

5. Safety

Electric checks include heating circuits, earthing, insulation and overtemperature. Gas systems additionally involve purge, ignition, flame supervision, pressure and rapid shutoff. Define the required functions in the actual control plan and applicable project documents.

6. Maintenance and production load

Assess electrical distribution and its maintenance for an electric option, and the gas supply station, exhaust and associated maintenance for a gas option. Include spare parts, maintenance capability, downtime and expansion conditions for both.

7. Life-cycle costs

Compare the same process, load, output, metering boundary and reporting period using local prices and actual duty. Installed power multiplied by hours, or rated gas flow multiplied by time, is only a rough estimate and does not replace measurement.

44.titleEn: Why Is a Trolley Furnace Heating Slowly? Check Eight Layers in Order
44.summaryEn: Establish a comparable curve before investigating loading, heat input, utilities, insulation, seals, circulation and measurement.
44.contentEn:
Slow heating does not necessarily mean insufficient rated power. Thermal load, effective input, heat losses, circulation, sensing and controls can all change the curve. Suneng's engineering team recommends establishing a comparable baseline and tracing the cause before treating a symptom as the fault.

A Suneng variable-capacity trolley-furnace proposal lists furnace-temperature points separately from workpiece-temperature points. For slow heating, first establish whether the furnace point is slow to reach its setpoint or a specified workpiece position is slow to reach its target. Compare records for the same load and time period. A control-screen screenshot needs the process curve, loading and measurement-point data; it cannot by itself establish insufficient heating power.

1. Operating curve: has heating actually become slower?

Place target and measured curves on the same time axis and identify where divergence starts. Compare equivalent workpieces, load, fixtures, starting temperature, target curve, equipment state, points and recording periods. Different conditions can explain a slower curve without an equipment failure.

2. Loading: has the thermal duty changed?

More material, thicker sections, heavier fixtures or denser stacking change heat demand and transfer. Physical fit does not mean the original heating conditions remain valid.

3. Heating output: rated capability is not actual input

For electric furnaces, review circuits, zone output and operating records. For gas furnaces, review pressure, flow, combustion, flame supervision and interlocks against the control plan. Competent personnel must perform hot, electrical and fuel-system checks under site procedures. If a safety-related abnormality appears, stop the diagnostic operation and follow equipment and site response procedures.

4. Utilities: compare consistent operating records

Upstream electricity or gas changes can limit output even if the furnace itself is sound. Compare the same metering boundary and time period with normal operation; an instantaneous reading cannot represent the whole heating cycle.

5. Lining: thermal images are clues

Damaged lining or insulation can increase loss. Combine visual inspection, thermography and repair history; one thermal image does not establish the extent of hidden damage.

6. Seals, pressure and exhaust

Door or trolley leakage, other openings and changes in furnace pressure or exhaust can increase losses. Assess seal structure with pressure and operating records. Visible leakage does not itself establish the root cause.

7. Circulation: only where fitted

If the furnace has fans and flow guides, review operation, rotation, guide condition and load obstruction together with heating, seals, loading and zones. Do not apply fan checks to a furnace without circulation equipment.

8. Sensing and controls

Check thermocouples, compensation wiring, instruments, zone outputs, programs and interlock states using calibration, trends and fault records. If the display and actual condition disagree, locate the cause rather than replace parts experimentally.

Eight-layer checklist

LayerRecordsInterpretation
CurveComparable target and measured history.Slow does not automatically mean faulty.
LoadingLayout and weights.Fit does not establish unchanged transfer.
HeatingOperation and alarms.Rated capacity is not effective input.
UtilitiesSame-period, same-boundary records.A snapshot is not a complete cycle.
LiningThermography and maintenance.Images guide further diagnosis.
Seals/pressurePressure and maintenance.Leakage does not prove its cause.
CirculationOperation and inspections.Applicable only to the installed arrangement.
Sensing/controlCalibration, trends and faults.Do not substitute trial replacement for diagnosis.

Verification after repair

Return as closely as practicable to the baseline duty and record target/measured curves, loading and energy input, with relevant interlock checks. Empty-furnace results establish only the functions tested and cannot be extended to all loads or processes.

Suneng provides assessments and retrofit support for operating furnaces, including overhauls, lining, seals, combustion and controls. Fault conclusions, work and improvement objectives follow the site tests, agreed proposal and contract. This framework does not replace operating procedures, risk assessment or site safety response.

43.titleEn: What Belongs in an Industrial Furnace Technical Agreement? Eight Clause Groups and Three Acceptance Boundaries
43.summaryEn: Turn operating inputs, supply responsibilities and test methods into an agreed, traceable technical baseline.
43.contentEn:
A technical agreement is more than a parameter list. It defines the design duty, deliverables, acceptance conditions and treatment of deviations. Suneng's engineering team groups common requirements into eight areas: operating inputs, equipment/performance, supply, utilities/interfaces, controls/safety, acceptance, documents and changes/service.

Suneng mesh-belt line documents allocate incoming wiring from the plant supply to the control-cabinet input, equipment-side wiring from the cabinet to equipment connections, and process commissioning separately. If a quotation says installation and commissioning are included, specify their boundaries, who prepares the site, who supplies test workpieces and who participates in process verification. Completed equipment connections and acceptable product-inspection results are separate matters, requiring separate evidence and responsibilities for resolving deviations.

Chapters can be combined or divided for the project. What matters is whether requirements are traceable, executable and testable, not the number of clauses. “Meets production needs,” “complete supply” and “stable operation” are insufficient on their own.

1. Operating inputs

Specify material, maximum dimensions, individual and batch weights, loading, fixtures, temperature, heating/holding, cooling, production cycle, annual hours and site energy, environment, logistics and layout. Together these determine type, effective zone, heat source, circulation, handling and controls. Size or maximum temperature alone rarely supports reliable selection.

2. Equipment and performance

Define type, systems, effective zone, temperature range, heating/circulation, handling, controls and safeguards. Attach measurement area, empty or loaded condition, points, instruments, recording interval, holding, data processing and evaluation to performance requirements. Record design targets, contractual guarantees and measurements separately; an untested target is not a measured result.

3. Supply scope

List the body, heating, circulation, mechanisms, controls, instruments, fixtures, supplied spares and special tools. Assign or exclude transport, unloading, lifting, foundations, secondary cables, trays, earthing, utilities, adjacent equipment, installation, commissioning and trials.

Suneng can define equipment interfaces across design, manufacture, installation, commissioning, retrofit and support. The actual inclusions follow the project agreement and contract. This scope discussion concerns engineering and supply responsibilities, not a legal determination of liability.

4. Utilities and interfaces

For water, electricity, gas and exhaust, state the medium, available capacity, connection point and form, responsible party and required completion time. Continuous lines also need cycle interlocks, workpiece handover, fault signals, emergency-stop links and data-communication boundaries. Confirm pressure, capacity and connection details for the actual site.

5. Controls and safety

Component brands do not describe functionality. Define temperature and program control, alarms and permissions; interlocks between overtemperature, sensor failure, fans, doors, mechanisms and energy; and safe states after loss of power, gas, water or communications. Specify recipe, curve, alarm, operation and batch records. Agree actual thresholds, interlock parameters and communication protocols for the system and site requirements.

6. Acceptance: distinguish three boundaries

  1. Targets, guarantees and measurements: design targets guide engineering, contractual guarantees define agreed obligations, and measured values come from specified tests.
  2. Factory and site acceptance: factory tests normally check manufacture, functions and agreed items before dispatch; site tests check installation, interfaces, integrated operation and agreed duty. State whether each is required, its scope, records and criteria.
  3. Chamber and effective working zone: geometric space is not automatically the agreed test/loading zone. Define the zone in words and drawings and locate workpieces, fixtures and points accordingly.

7. Documents, training and spares

List general arrangement, foundations, interfaces, electrical documents, operating/maintenance instructions, wear parts, conformity documents, test records and agreed software/parameter backups. Specify format, language, submission stage and confirmation responsibility. Training needs defined participants, content, location and completion evidence. Separate included spares, special tools and parts available for later purchase.

8. Changes and service

Changes to workpieces, process, output, layout or utilities need a record of content, impact, approver and effective version. Installation assistance, commissioning, training, fault support and spares require project-specific scope, response arrangements and completion criteria.

Technical-agreement checklist

GroupCheckCommon omission
InputsWorkpiece, process, load, cycle and site.Only chamber dimensions.
Equipment/performanceSystems, zone, targets and test conditions.Numbers without methods.
SupplyInclusions, exclusions, parts and tools.“Complete equipment” without a list.
Utilities/interfacesMedium, capacity, connections and owners.Only “customer supplies utilities.”
Controls/safetyFunctions, interlocks, abnormal states and data.Brands alone.
AcceptanceFactory/site scope, state, instruments, records and criteria.Targets mixed with measurements.
DocumentsDrawings, manuals, lists, records and training.No format or submission stage.
Changes/serviceVersions, deviations, support and completion.Unrecorded verbal changes.

Three final checks

Every performance statement needs applicable conditions; every supply item needs an owner; every acceptance conclusion needs a consistent method and criterion. This is a general engineering checklist, not a project agreement or legal advice. Confirm standard versions, targets, scope, tests and services in the formal project documents.

42.titleEn: Five Checks for a Variable-volume Trolley Furnace Proposal for Pressure Vessels
42.summaryEn: Use this historical proposal to check rear-wall position, effective heating zones, burner controls, seals, temperature records and verification scope.
42.contentEn:
Review a variable-volume trolley furnace proposal for pressure vessels in five parts: rear wall and effective zone, burner control, seals, furnace/workpiece measurements and verification by zone. The historical Suneng proposal records three effective zones and their configuration. These records support procurement questions; configuration alone establishes neither a fixed saving nor the control and acceptance plan for a new project.

This article draws on Suneng's variable-volume gas-fired trolley-furnace proposal dated 27 April 2020. The proposal does not establish delivery or acceptance. The customer remains anonymous. Dimensions, loading, temperatures, zones and test figures below are the proposal's inputs and agreed targets; the article does not reproduce individual final test measurements or offer a universal configuration.

Which effective heating lengths does the proposal record?

The furnace was specified for post-weld stress relief of pressure vessels and other weldments. The physical chamber is 15.3 × 7.3 × 7.15 m, the door opening 7 × 7 m and the trolley deck 15 × 7 m. The proposed maximum load is 200 tonnes, excluding heat treatment support saddles.

The movable rear wall provides effective heating zones of 5 × 7 × 7 m, 10 × 7 × 7 m and 15 × 7 × 7 m, selected for the occupied workpiece length. Reduced heated space does not translate directly into a fixed saving: fuel use also depends on weight, material, starting temperature, curve, holding, utilisation, seals and metering boundary.

1. Rear-wall position and the corresponding effective zone

Check the recorded rear wall, trolley, sealing mechanisms and controls together. Match each wall position to its corresponding effective heating area. The movement method, seal structure and actuator quantities belong to this project and cannot be copied directly to other furnace dimensions.

2. Control documents for each effective zone

The gas-fired proposal specifies 12 burner assemblies and 12 furnace-temperature control zones. Request combustion and control descriptions for each effective-zone setting; burner count alone does not establish the active range. Check how the documents relate rear-wall position, combustion zones, doors, trolley, seals and safety interlocks. Operating permissions, switching and abnormal responses follow this equipment’s technical documents and controlled procedures. These are project quantities, not universal requirements.

3. Sealing descriptions for each rear-wall position

Match the 5 m and 10 m rear-wall positions separately to the proposal’s sealing descriptions. Ask the supplier to identify each position’s seal arrangement and verification conditions. A drawing for the maximum effective zone cannot replace descriptions for every position.

4. Furnace control and workpiece temperature records are different

The 12 furnace-temperature control zones are accompanied by 16 workpiece-thermocouple channels with display, recording and alarms. Furnace sensing controls the heating zones; workpiece sensing follows actual temperatures at selected locations. Sixteen channels is a project configuration, and point number and position require the workpiece, dimensions, layout, process and test method.

The historical proposal lists control-point accuracy as “±1°C” and the holding-temperature target as “≤±10°C (at or above 550°C)”, with measurement at the end of holding noted separately. These are proposal targets, not measured results. The 550°C threshold belongs to this proposal and is not a universal minimum survey temperature.

The proposal cited the 2012 method; this article explains the current method in GB/T 9452-2023. Correct readings for the sensor, compensation cable and instrument, then subtract the test-zone setpoint from each actual temperature. Compare the maximum and minimum deviations with the process limits. Highest-minus-lowest spread is not a substitute, and the “±1°C” control target does not establish work-zone uniformity. The survey must also meet data-collection and test-validity requirements; an end-of-hold reading or an average alone is insufficient. If a point fails the original process target, adjust and resurvey.

5. Effective zones and conditions covered by the report

GB/T 9452-2023 requires separate surveys for different qualified work zones. For the proposed 5 m, 10 m and 15 m settings, match each report to rear-wall position, active burner zones, seals and loading. Record test temperatures and setpoints, sensor positions, calibration corrections, sampling times, upper/lower deviations and conclusions for each setting. Records for the 15 m state alone do not establish temperature conformity for the other settings.

The original plan includes cold and hot commissioning, uniformity and energy-efficiency tests, followed by 1–2 trial-production batches. These describe the planned verification scope; no individual measured test values are supplied here. A new project can use the current method described above, with process tolerances and work zones specified in its technical agreement. The new edition does not retrospectively change the historical proposal or establish its acceptance.

Project parameters and boundaries

ItemProposalBoundary
WorkpiecesPressure vessels and other weldments of varying sizes.Post-weld stress relief, not every vessel treatment.
Effective zones5 m, 10 m and 15 m lengths; 7 × 7 m cross-section.Specific trolley and rear-wall structure.
Maximum load200 tonnes excluding heat treatment support saddles.Confirm load distribution, supports and rails.
Operating/design temperature800°C operating; 850°C maximum design.Equipment parameters, not a recommended treatment temperature.
Furnace control12 burners and 12 zones.Recalculate for another thermal duty.
Workpiece sensing16 channels with records and alarms.Locate points for the workpiece and process.
Temperature targetsControl point ±1°C; source holding-temperature notation ≤±10°C at or above 550°C, measured at the end of holding.Historical targets. Compare corrected survey readings with the test setpoint; an end-of-hold reading alone is insufficient.
Acceptance planCold/hot commissioning, uniformity, efficiency and 1–2 trial batches.Methods and criteria require project agreement.

Supply responsibilities and enquiry inputs

In this project, Suneng is responsible for furnace design, manufacture, installation, cold/hot commissioning and inspection/testing, excluding civil foundations. The customer supplies foundations, building, utilities, low-voltage cable connection, gas conditions and fixtures. Other projects follow their own contracts.

Provide product, grade, dimensions, individual and total load, support saddles and layout, the batch mix by size, complete post-weld treatment curves, measurement requirements, utilities, building/foundation constraints and acceptance for each chamber state. Size mix and loading frequency directly affect whether variable volume is worthwhile.

Suneng can compare fixed and variable-volume trolley proposals and define the effective zones, wall/seals, burners, records and supply boundary. Final parameters follow the agreed technical documents.
