41.titleEn: Five Checks for a Bulldozer Blade Roller-hearth Quenching Furnace Proposal
41.summaryEn: Use this historical proposal to check conveying, temperature zones, circulation and measurement, press interfaces and supply responsibilities.
41.contentEn:
Review a bulldozer-blade roller-hearth quenching proposal in five parts: conveying, heating zones, circulation and measurement, discharge interfaces, and supply/acceptance. The historical Suneng proposal records these configurations and interfaces. Match them to this project’s workpieces, treatment and quenching press; maximum temperature or power alone is insufficient for selection.

This article explains a Suneng roller-hearth quenching-furnace technical proposal prepared in 2020. The proposal does not establish delivery or acceptance. Customer information remains anonymous. The dimensions, power, zones and temperature figures below describe the project's design inputs and agreed targets; this article does not reproduce the individual final test measurements. They are not standard values for every roller-hearth furnace.

Match the recorded workpiece and process path

The proposal covers bulldozer blades and similar elongated plate parts, with input dimensions of 260–3,000 mm long, 100–550 mm wide and 12–120 mm thick. After heating and holding, parts transfer quickly to the customer's press-quenching machine.

The design must establish stable entry, travel through heating and equalising zones for different lengths and thicknesses, rapid discharge and the movement and responsibility interfaces between furnace, discharge equipment and press. Specifying a “950°C quenching furnace” alone does not answer these questions. The proposal combines continuous rollers, five control zones, circulation in the middle/rear equalising section and an independently driven rapid-discharge section.

1. Conveying and workpiece support

The proposal combines continuous roller conveying with rapid discharge. Compare conveying paths, support, cycle and the press interface separately. The configuration description alone does not rank roller-hearth, trolley or other furnace types.

Assess hot-workpiece support and stability; entry, dwell and exit timing across the size range; door opening relative to thickness; access for individual roller replacement; and speed transition between slow furnace travel and rapid discharge. The independent outlet drive is specific to this project and does not establish universal roller counts, drive sections or speeds.

2. Match temperature-zone configuration to the process

The proposed working chamber is 12,000 × 570 × 160 mm, with maximum working temperature 950°C, rated heating power 400 kW and five independent temperature-control zones. Five zones establishes zoned control, but does not by itself establish each zone’s process duty or the number needed for another project.

Ask for the project’s zone description linked to workpiece length and thickness, product changes, conveying speed and residence time, heater arrangement, thermal load, door disturbances, heating rate, holding and records. The historical five-zone, 400 kW configuration is not a general selection conclusion; a new project needs its own process inputs and design.

3. Define circulation, sealing and measurement objects

Zones 3, 4 and 5 each have one high-temperature circulation fan. Circulation improves heat exchange around the parts, but uniformity also depends on element distribution and zone output; roof, wall and roller-penetration seals; inlet/outlet door conditions; loading, spacing and shielding; and thermocouple positions, test state and calculation method.

The historical proposal lists uniformity as “≤±7.5°C” and control accuracy as “≤±1°C”. These are proposal targets, not measured proof of achieved performance; a control target cannot replace a qualified-work-zone temperature survey.

For the current assessment method, GB/T 9452-2023 uses readings corrected for the sensor, compensation cable and instrument. Subtract the test-zone temperature setpoint from each actual temperature, then compare the maximum and minimum deviations with the process limits. The highest-minus-lowest temperature spread cannot replace these setpoint-referenced checks.

For a continuous roller-hearth furnace, first identify the survey zones with a fixed process heating temperature and a uniformity requirement. A zone falls outside this standard’s qualified-work-zone test if it lacks a fixed process heating temperature or has no uniformity requirement. Five control zones do not automatically form one constant-temperature work zone. Match records to each survey zone’s setpoint, loading, conveying and door state, and meet the data-collection and test-validity requirements; one reading or an average cannot establish conformity. If a point fails the original process target, adjust and resurvey. This explains the current method, not additional measured evidence for the 2020 project. Neither the historical targets nor the three-fan arrangement transfer automatically to another chamber, load or temperature condition.

4. Discharge actions and the press interface

The proposal links infrared arrival detection, rear-door opening, activation of the independent rapid-discharge drive and transfer to the customer-supplied quenching press. Uncontrolled transfer can change the workpiece's thermal state before pressing.

Agree the permitted transfer window; outlet and press height, centreline and speed; arrival, door, drive and press-ready interlocks; safe responses to failed discharge, an unpositioned door or an unavailable press; and responsibilities for quench water, circulation piping and integrated commissioning. The source proposal does not establish a fixed transfer time for all projects.

5. Supply scope and interface responsibility

Suneng designs and supplies the roller-hearth furnace. In this project, the customer provides loading and discharge racks and the quenching press, quench water/circulation and specified utility connections. This is a technical integration boundary, not only a commercial attachment.

A furnace may operate individually while the line cannot complete its sequence if the press state, rack centreline, water capacity, compressed air and power connections are unresolved. Assign equipment, actions, signals, utilities, installation, commissioning, trial loads and acceptance, with inputs and documents. Other projects require their own responsibility agreement.

Project parameters and their limits

ItemProposalInterpretation
WorkpieceBulldozer blades and similar elongated plate parts.Furnace selection follows both the workpiece and press-quench route.
Working chamber12,000 × 570 × 160 mm.Specific to the project arrangement.
Maximum working temperature950°C.Not the operating temperature for every recipe.
Rated heating power400 kW.Requires thermal-load, cycle and loss calculations.
Control zones5.Confirm each zone’s duty against the project process.
Internal roller speed0–20 m/min.Adjustment range, not a fixed process speed.
CirculationFans in the three middle/rear zones.Assess with heating, sealing, loading and sensing.
Temperature targetsSource notation: uniformity ≤±7.5°C; control accuracy ≤±1°C.Historical targets. Assess corrected survey readings against the test setpoint; check the control item separately.

Acceptance covers the furnace and process chain

The source proposal calls for an agreed acceptance outline and 3–5 heat treatment trial batches after site commissioning, including blade hardness, hardness uniformity, microstructure and flatness checks. It separates equipment functions—mechanisms, doors, rollers, heating, sensing, records, alarms and interlocks—from workpiece verification under the agreed material, load, heating, transfer and press-quench conditions.

Initial material, loading, transfer, pressing pressure, cooling medium, sampling and inspection also affect hardness, structure and flatness. The acceptance outline must assign guarantees and evaluation responsibilities rather than attribute every product result automatically to the furnace supplier.

When this design approach is relevant

Consider it for elongated plate parts needing continuous or indexed movement, heating/holding, rapid discharge and press quenching, where different sizes can share a support reference and the furnace must coordinate with downstream equipment. The buyer needs workpiece, curve, cycle, transfer and press-interface data.

Complex shapes, difficult supports, highly variable loading or long complete-batch holding may favour trolley, box or other furnaces. A quenching requirement alone does not establish roller-hearth suitability.

Enquiry inputs

Prepare material, size range, individual weight, flatness target, loading orientation, curve, cycle, upstream/downstream flow, permitted transfer time, press interface, utilities and acceptance. Suneng can assess the furnace, controls and supply responsibilities from these inputs. Confirm dimensions, power, zones, speeds, temperature targets, interfaces and tests in the technical agreement.

40.titleEn: Retrofit or Replace an Old Trolley Furnace? Compare These Four Cost and Capability Areas
40.summaryEn: Review recoverable condition, process fit, operating costs and implementation over the same life-cycle boundary.
40.contentEn:
Do not decide whether to retrofit an old trolley furnace from age, one repair bill or a theoretical saving alone. First assess recoverable structure and safety, then fit with the new process and capacity, then energy, failures and maintenance, and finally shutdown, construction, restart and life-cycle costs against replacement.

A Suneng solution-treatment furnace relocation proposal retains mechanical equipment but still renews controls, limits and hearth supports. Include reuse checks, interface changes, dismantling, reassembly and restart verification when comparing total retrofit and replacement costs. If the quotation lists only new parts, first add the site work and conditions for restoring production. Work left out of a quotation is not a demonstrated saving.

This article separates fault repair, complete overhaul, system retrofit and replacement before comparing four groups of costs and conditions. The framework supports a site-diagnosis checklist; it does not replace equipment safety assessment, technical agreements or investment approval.

Define the work before naming it

ActionPurposeTypical boundary
Fault repairRestore a failed component or action.Original design and main targets broadly unchanged.
Complete overhaulRestore structure, lining, drives, heating or controls.Recover reliability and usable life.
System retrofitAddress control, sealing, circulation, combustion, automation or capacity bottlenecks.Process objectives, interfaces or acceptance change.
ReplacementMeet new process/output or resolve structural limitations.Redefine the equipment and delivery proposal.

A motor, instrument or local lining replacement may be repair or overhaul. Redesigning heating, circulation, seals, controls, trolley loading and interlocks calls for system-level assessment. The label cannot replace a scope definition.

1. How far can structure and safety be restored?

Inspect body, foundations, trolley, rails, door, seals, drives, lining, heat source, sensing and interlocks. Investigate continuing distortion, cracks, corrosion and load risks; repairability of rails, wheels, drives and doors; suitability of retained lining, seals and interfaces; restoration of applicable fuel, electrical, overtemperature, thermocouple-break, emergency-stop and movement safeguards; and parts, documents and maintainability.

If structural risks remain, critical parts are not recoverable or the retained system would continue to limit the process, formally compare replacement. Age is only a clue: a well-maintained recoverable furnace is not equivalent to one with repeated overload, piecemeal repairs and missing records merely because their years of service match.

2. How large is the gap to the new process and output?

ItemVerify the existing stateDefine the target
Workpieces/loadingMaterial, dimensions, weights, fixtures and load.New specification range and maximum load.
CurveTemperatures, heating, holding, cooling and records.New curves, zones and traceability.
Temperature/controlZone, points, instruments, circulation and seals.Test state, method and criteria.
Output/cycleActual batch cycle, shifts, waiting and faults.Target cycle, shifts and annual output.
Automation/interfacesControls, programs, communications and adjacent equipment.Recipes, data, coordinated operation and safety.

An overhaul may suffice to restore the original duty. A focused or system retrofit may suit a local bottleneck with manageable interfaces. If chamber, loading, energy and process route all change, the work can approach remanufacturing and should be compared with a new furnace.

A new instrument or cabinet cannot automatically establish uniformity, output or product quality. Sensing, heating zones, circulation, lining, seals, loading and settings also matter.

3. Are operation, failures and maintenance manageable?

Collect a representative reporting period covering actual loads, product mix, curves and shifts; electricity, fuel and other metering boundaries; heating, holding, standby and empty time; fault types, counts, downtime and parts; rework, reheating, scheduling interruptions and maintenance labour; and losses through doors, lining, exhaust or cooling.

Compare savings, deviation, output, faults or unit-product energy using the same duty, metering boundary, reporting period and agreed method. Without a baseline, identify improvement directions rather than promise a percentage.

Also assess spare-parts availability and maintenance capability. Obsolete components, inaccessible programs and improvised replacements can create downtime risks greater than the visible repair cost.

4. Compare shutdown, implementation and life-cycle costs

A lower retrofit quotation does not necessarily mean a lower total cost. Include survey, design, prefabrication, removal, installation and commissioning; retained-system uncertainties and extra work; lost production, backup capacity, restart verification and contingency arrangements; expected remaining life, maintenance and future upgrades; new-furnace manufacture, foundations, utilities, changeover and old-equipment disposal; and energy, maintenance and downtime over the same evaluation period.

Separate survey, design and prefabrication that can be completed before shutdown from removal, tie-ins and installation that require the furnace to stop. Then schedule cold checks, heating, loaded verification and restart observation for the project. Do not create apparent on-time completion by omitting necessary tests. Adjust scope, phase the work or use a suitable planned maintenance period.

A decision matrix

FindingDirection to assess first
One component failed; structure and process objectives remain suitable.Fault repair.
Lining, drives, heating or controls aged; original process still applies.Complete overhaul.
Main structure usable; bottleneck and interfaces manageable.System retrofit.
High structural/safety risk or unrecoverable critical components.Replacement.
Major changes in workpieces, load, process, energy and controls.Compare retrofit and new equipment in parallel.
Work approaches remanufacturing while retained risks remain substantial.Give replacement particular consideration.

This selects the next assessment, not a final investment decision. The conclusion needs documents, diagnosis, risks, scope and a comparable cost model.

What Suneng can assess

Suneng can assess its own equipment and some other-brand furnaces for overhaul, modification, relocation/restart and energy improvements. Review starts with records, site condition, process objectives, energy, faults, shutdown and safety, then defines repair, retrofit or replacement boundaries. Type, structure, location and site risks determine whether the work can be accepted.

Quantified savings, deviation, output gains, fixed schedules and payback require a site diagnosis, baseline and test method. Calibration, emissions tests or third-party certification require appropriately qualified bodies under the project's applicable requirements.

Common questions

At what age should a trolley furnace be replaced?

There is no universal threshold. Check design margins, duty, maintenance, structure, components, process changes and risk.

At what percentage of new-equipment cost should a retrofit be rejected?

No single ratio applies. Align scope, life, shutdown, energy, maintenance, risk and the evaluation period.

Will changing controls fix slow heating and uneven temperature?

Not necessarily. Check heating, combustion, airflow, lining, seals, loading, sensing and the process program first.

Can assessment start without complete drawings?

Yes, with a gap review and possible field measurements. Missing structural, loading, utility or control information limits proposal accuracy and risk assessment.

Information for an initial assessment

Provide type, manufacture and modification years, chamber size, workpieces and load, curves, energy, installed power and actual consumption, faults, temperature records, controls, photographs, target process/output and shutdown. Email 997518512@qq.com or call +86-130-5298-6814.

39.titleEn: Choosing a Trolley Furnace Manufacturer: Five Types of Capability Evidence
39.summaryEn: Verify comparable duty, design, manufacturing, acceptance and service before relying on factory size, certificates or price.
39.contentEn:
First establish whether a supplier has handled workpieces, loads, processes, energy sources and acceptance boundaries comparable to yours. Then examine design documents, manufacturing, delivery and support. Factory buildings, certificates, customer names and low prices are useful context, but none alone establishes suitability.

Suneng trolley-furnace retrofit documents place the added section, integration with the original controls and whole-furnace retesting within one scope. Use that relationship to check that a candidate's design, manufacturing and acceptance documents describe the same equipment version. If the drawing shows a longer chamber but the test plan covers only the original working zone, request an aligned revision. More documents do not necessarily mean consistent documents.

Suneng's engineering team groups the evidence into comparable duty, design, manufacturing, acceptance/delivery and after-sales support. The framework applies to all candidates, including Suneng, and is not a ranking.

1. Is the reference project actually comparable?

The same furnace name can conceal very different equipment boundaries. Compare material, maximum dimensions, individual weight and loading; treatment, usual/maximum temperatures, heating, holding and cooling; batch load, shifts, cycle and output; electric or gas heating and utilities; effective zone, temperature records, uniformity and traceability; trolley capacity, seals, circulation, movements and interlocks; and factory testing, transport, installation, site commissioning and final handover.

A photograph or customer name does not establish these similarities. Under appropriate confidentiality arrangements, ask for the supply scope, similarities, differences and verifiable records while protecting customer drawings, programs and prices.

2. Design capability appears in documents

EvidenceWhat to check
Requirement confirmationWorkpiece, loading, process, output, energy, controls, acceptance and site.
Loading or arrangement drawingWorkpieces, fixtures, effective zone, load capacity and handling/maintenance space.
Key calculation summaryInputs for thermal load or power, structure, circulation, zones and cycle.
System/control descriptionHeat source, flow guides, seals, records, alarms and interlocks matched to duty.
Draft acceptance planWhich performance is checked at the factory or site, with records and criteria.

A custom trolley design requires those inputs. Dimensions without workpieces, load, curves and acceptance cannot reliably fix capacity, heating, zones, circulation and delivery scope.

3. Manufacturing capability needs process evidence

Possible witness points include frozen design and supply lists; body, trolley, doors and key materials; lining, seals, heating/combustion and circulation; cabinet, wiring, instruments, program versions and interlocks; and cold movements, empty-furnace heating, records and issue closure.

Choose points for the project's risks rather than maximising their number. Heavy loads place more emphasis on trolley, rails and drives. Demanding temperature distribution places more emphasis on zones, circulation, seals, measurement points and records. Electric and gas versions need their own relevant safety checks.

4. Define acceptance and delivery before comparing prices

The agreement should identify document and standard versions; separate factory and site scopes; temperatures, load state, points, instruments, stabilisation and recording; pass criteria, corrective work, retests and closure; responsibilities for transport, unloading, foundations, rails, utilities, exhaust, installation and commissioning; and delivery of training, drawings, programs, spares and documents.

Uniformity results require the effective zone and complete measurement conditions, not a universal isolated number. Factory pre-acceptance does not complete acceptance after transport, installation and utility connection.

5. Make after-sales terms executable

Specify fault-reporting channels, required information and initial response; remote and site support and each party's cooperation; wear and critical spare parts, alternatives and supply scope; program, password, parameter and version management; attribution of issues caused by operation, maintenance, material, utilities or environment; and warranty start, charges and support inside and outside warranty.

Distance may help communication, but it is not a response commitment. Put methods, information, responsibility and costs in the contract.

38.titleEn: What Should Trolley Furnace Acceptance Cover?
38.summaryEn: Use seven connected checks for agreed documents, manufacturing, interlocks, temperature, loaded operation and site handover.
38.contentEn:
Trolley-furnace acceptance should match records to the agreed structure, movements, safety, temperature control, uniformity, loaded operation and delivery responsibilities, then check whether the actual results meet the agreed requirements. Address incomplete or failed items and limitations separately; a complete set of documents does not establish acceptance. Demonstrating that the furnace heats up is insufficient. The contract, technical agreement, supply list and acceptance plan define the work; test conditions and criteria vary by project.

A Suneng variable-capacity trolley-furnace proposal lists furnace-temperature points separately from workpiece-temperature points. When receiving a temperature curve, identify the connected measurement point and test run before deciding whether it describes furnace control or workpiece heating. If the loading and point relationship is missing, request a channel list, point layout and common batch identifier. A smooth curve alone cannot establish completion of all acceptance checks.

One Suneng proposal describes factory pre-acceptance, site installation, individual and integrated commissioning, empty and loaded trials, training and documents. Other projects may use different stages and sequences. The engineering team groups procurement checks into seven levels below; this framework helps prepare a project checklist and does not replace the contract or applicable standards.

1. Acceptance basis: freeze document versions

Confirm the versions and precedence of the contract and technical agreement; supply list and inclusions/exclusions; general arrangement, foundations and utility conditions; test items, states, methods and criteria; instruments, sensors and recorders; and deviation, correction, retest and signature procedures.

Identify applicable standard versions and clauses in the agreement. Relevant categories can include manufacturing, temperature measurement, electrical safety and, where applicable, fuel safety and emissions. This article does not prescribe one universal set of standard numbers for every trolley furnace. Workpiece, loading, temperature, curve, energy, controls and site conditions determine the checklist.

2. Manufacturing and assembly: compare the equipment with the approved design

Check the body, lining, door, trolley and drive against the drawings; rails, limits, seals and mechanisms for intended operation; heating, circulation, temperature controls and cabinet completeness; nameplates, instruments, major components and safety parts against the list; welding, insulation, seals, finish and maintenance access; and supplied spares, special tools and accessories.

Where required, review material certificates, bought-in component documents and manufacturing records. Appearance alone does not establish structural, configuration or document conformity.

3. Movements and interlocks: include abnormal conditions

Test the agreed sequence for trolley travel, door movement, sealing, fans and heating or combustion permissives. Verify normal start, stop and reset; direction, limits and mutual interlocks; fan/heating/door permissives; overtemperature, thermocouple-break and emergency-stop protection; power-loss, restoration and interruption states; and traceable alarms, trends and operating records.

Record the tests. One successful normal movement does not prove the fault logic. Gas-fired versions also need their specified purge, ignition, pressure, rapid shutoff, flame-supervision and combustion-fan checks. Electric versions require their specified heating circuits, overtemperature protection, earthing and insulation checks. The two heat sources should not share an inappropriate generic combustion checklist.

4. Empty-furnace control: examine the curve

Define the test temperature and program, empty or other agreed condition, zone controls and records, stabilisation and observation period, alarm and overshoot recording, evaluation and retest conditions.

The test checks heating, zones, displays, trends and operation in the agreed state. A single endpoint screenshot cannot replace complete heating and holding curves. This section locates the empty-furnace test within whole-equipment acceptance; the factory-test plan should detail the relevant manufacturing, interlock and pre-dispatch checks.

5. Temperature uniformity: a deviation number needs context

There is no single uniformity value for all trolley furnaces. Bind the result to the effective working zone, test temperatures, no-load or loaded state, point number and arrangement, stabilisation, measurement/recording/calculation method, instrument and sensor condition, and pass/retest rules.

Suneng can support contracted uniformity tests and control-system accuracy checks. Metrological calibration or third-party certification requires appropriately qualified organisations. Factory-stage testing does not automatically replace installed-site acceptance. The project-specific uniformity plan should define point positions, quantities and calculations.

6. Loaded trials: verify the agreed duty

If included, use confirmed workpieces or an equivalent load, fixtures, layout, curve and recording method. Check trolley loading and travel; loaded heating, holding and zone records; stable doors, seals, circulation and heat source; handling cycle, transfer and unloading against production arrangements; and who performs workpiece temperature measurement or product inspection and by which method.

Meeting furnace-temperature criteria does not automatically establish every hardness, microstructure or distortion result. Material condition, prior processing, loading, transfer, cooling and inspection also affect the product. Define those responsibilities in the technical agreement.

7. Site handover: factory acceptance is not the end

After delivery, check foundations, rails, crane and access, water/electricity/gas/exhaust interfaces and installed individual and integrated operation. Handover should address installation and commissioning records; operation, maintenance and abnormal-condition training; assembly, electrical and layout/foundation drawings; manuals; supply, wear-part and spare-part lists; and remaining issues, owners, deadlines, retests and closure evidence.

Document types and quantities vary by project. One proposal's document package is not a default specification for every furnace.

Common questions

Does passing empty-furnace heating complete acceptance?

No. It covers only part of the agreed control and operation checks, not all interlocks, uniformity, loaded trials, installation and documents.

Why test again after factory pre-acceptance?

Transport, installation, foundations, rails and actual utilities can change the state. Verify installed interfaces, movements and the contracted site tests.

Should uniformity be tested at the factory or on site?

Follow the technical agreement. Factory verification may establish an agreed pre-dispatch state; the site retest requirement depends on the installed conditions and contracted boundary.

Does a receipt or signature prove performance?

It proves the receipt or approval stated in that document, not automatically uniformity, energy use, life or every process property.

37.titleEn: Choosing a Furnace Retrofit Supplier in Jiangsu: Establish Condition and a Baseline First
37.summaryEn: Check site diagnosis, work scope, shutdown planning and comparable acceptance tests before accepting performance promises.
37.contentEn:
Check whether a retrofit supplier will carry out site diagnosis as required by the project. Where energy, temperature, output or failure-rate targets are quantified, check whether it will establish a comparable baseline. It should distinguish repairs from system changes, organise the shutdown work and close acceptance with comparable tests. Without those conditions, energy savings, temperature deviation, duration and payback should not become firm promises.

A Suneng solution-treatment furnace relocation proposal distinguishes the reused fork mechanism, renewed electrical controls and limits, and new hearth supports. Ask a retrofit supplier to mark retained and changed positions on the existing arrangement and explain how old and new interfaces will be checked. A list of new parts alone needs the installation connections and restart-verification scope before it represents a comparable complete job.

Suneng publishes this procurement-checking method and is a potential equipment-side provider. This article does not rank other companies or make unsupported third-party comparisons.

Distinguish repair, overhaul, retrofit and replacement

Complete overhaulRestore structure, lining, drives, heating or controls.Remaining life, inspection scope, wear parts and restart verification.

Relocation/restartMove, reinstall and reverify equipment.Identification, packaging, foundations, utilities and recommissioning.
ReplacementMeet new process/output or address structural limitations.Life-cycle costs, interruption and changeover.

Compare replacement alongside retrofit if the structure is badly distorted, safety risks are high, critical parts cannot be restored, the process has changed substantially or retained interfaces would continue to constrain the new proposal.

Six steps from diagnosis to acceptance

1. Review documents and identify gaps

Prepare drawings, type and dimensions, material and loading, curves, controls, fault history, energy bills, temperature records, photographs, shifts and the shutdown window. The supplier should identify what can be measured on site and what missing information prevents design freeze.

2. Trace symptoms to system causes

Inspect structure and foundations, lining, doors and seals, heating/combustion, circulation and guides, drives, temperature instruments, controls/interlocks, utilities and operating practice. Uneven temperature, slow heating and high consumption often have multiple causes. Photographs alone cannot establish a final work list.

3. Establish the pre-retrofit baseline

For energy, uniformity, output or fault-rate targets, define measurement points, reporting period, loading, shifts, environment, test state and abnormal-data treatment before work. Otherwise, equipment changes cannot be separated reliably from production or reporting changes.

4. Write the scope, interfaces and exclusions

List retained, removed, repaired and added items. Assign responsibilities at the old structure, cabinet, piping, foundations, flues, fixtures, adjacent equipment and customer utilities. For third-party equipment or software, confirm programs, communication protocols, spares and site authorisation. Interfaces requiring unauthorised programs or protocols must remain outside the agreed retrofit scope until access is properly authorised.

5. Plan backwards from the shutdown window

Use the allowed start and finish to schedule survey, design, prefabrication, material arrival, removal, installation, wiring, cold checks, heating, loaded verification and restart observation. Continuous plants may consider work by line or section or during planned maintenance, subject to site safety and production arrangements.

6. Verify under comparable conditions

Acceptance may cover movements and interlocks, heating, temperature stability/uniformity, drives, seals, records, protection, recipe execution and agreed energy or emissions targets. Quantified comparisons require equivalent duty, metering boundaries and reporting periods. Define emissions indicators, methods and responsibilities under the applicable project requirements. In China, a pollution-discharging entity with the necessary conditions and capability may carry out self-monitoring as permitted by law or commission a qualified testing or monitoring body. Where a legally recognised evidentiary report is required, verify the body’s accreditation and authorised scope. See HJ 819-2017, section 4.3 for the organisation of self-monitoring in China.

If a proposal promises fixed savings, deviation, duration or payback from a few photographs, request its assumptions, measurement methods and conditions.

What a public retrofit case can establish

Suneng's public stainless-steel continuous-line retrofit reference explains published project specifications, stage durations, system arrangements, calculation boundaries and acceptance methods. The customer remains anonymous; contract value and operating results not authorised for disclosure are not included.

The design and calculations belong to the original furnace, fuel, line load, insulation, controls and operation. Another furnace needs a new site baseline, energy model and acceptance plan; the original numbers cannot simply be transferred.

Its retrofit work can include site diagnosis, design and interfaces, components and systems, support for dismantling/installation, commissioning and service. It can assess its own equipment and some other-brand furnaces for overhaul, modification, relocation/restart and energy improvements after obtaining the equipment records and inspecting the site.

Feasibility depends on type, structure, process objectives, documents, location, shutdown, safety and responsibilities. Quantified savings, temperature deviation, schedule, payback or output require diagnosis, a baseline and a test method. Record such targets together with their conditions in the technical agreement.

Common questions

Can assessment begin with incomplete documents?

Yes, by identifying gaps. Provide the known furnace, workpiece, curve, faults, energy, photographs and shutdown information; key values may still require measurement.

Will new controls solve uneven temperature?

Not necessarily. Sensing, zones, circulation, lining, seals, loading and settings can all contribute.

How should savings be written into a contract?

Define the baseline period, load, product, meters, energy conversion, environment, downtime treatment and post-retrofit test and evaluation before agreeing a percentage.

Is one empty-furnace test enough?

It can verify some movements and heating. Capacity, process and operating targets may also require a defined load, continuous run or sample verification.

Can work fit a very short shutdown?

Compare the available window with construction and restart verification. Move incompatible work to planned maintenance or assess phased implementation; site and supply conditions determine the schedule.

Can another manufacturer's furnace be assessed?

Yes, initially. Records, site diagnosis, structure, type, location, shutdown and safety determine whether the work can be accepted.

Eight inputs that define the task

  1. Material, specification range, individual weight and loading.
  2. The required treatment, such as annealing, normalizing, quenching, tempering, solution treatment, ageing, carburizing or nitriding.
  3. Maximum/usual temperatures, heating/cooling curve and holding.

  7. Effective zone, uniformity, records and process-result verification.
  8. Transport, foundations, installation, commissioning, training, spares, warranty and service location.

Incomplete inputs support only a conditional direction. Comparing totals at that stage can mistake an incomplete scope for a lower-cost proposal.

Technical discussions should cover material, the workpiece range, loading, curves, output, energy, quality and interfaces, not only chamber dimensions. Request a requirement-confirmation sheet and an assumptions list. The sheet records known inputs; unresolved assumptions cannot be treated as a final quotation basis.

2. A traceable thermal and structural design

Review the effective zone, loading, heat balance or power selection, circulation, load capacity, drives, door seals, insulation and maintenance access. Continuous lines also require cycle, buffer, abnormal-material and upstream/downstream interface checks. Document completeness and logical consistency do not replace the process owner's confirmation of product results.

3. Temperature and process controls expressed as test conditions

For uniformity, specify zone, temperature, load, points, stabilisation, recording, instruments, evaluation and retests. Apply the same combination of target, conditions, method and responsibility to atmosphere, carbon potential, vacuum, quenching and traceability.

4. Manufacturing and quality records

Check materials and bought-in components, welding and assembly stages, lining, seals, heating or combustion, drives, instrument calibration, program backups and deviation records. Factory scale and videos are supporting context, not substitutes for project records. Check that records concern this project, results meet the agreed requirements and deviations have been resolved. The existence of records does not establish manufacturing conformity, and manufacturing checks do not guarantee the final process result.

5. Distinct factory and site acceptance

Factory acceptance normally checks the agreed equipment, movements, interlocks, heating, records and tests before dispatch. Site acceptance checks the installed equipment under actual utilities and integrated conditions. Define scope, samples, duration, responsibilities and deviation closure for both. Passing the factory test does not complete the site test.

6. Delivery and after-sales responsibilities

A responsibility matrix is a table showing what each party must supply, connect, support and verify. Include the equipment supplier, customer and other participants, covering foundations, utilities, lifting, installation, commissioning materials, trials, training, spares and service. The supplier is responsible for the contracted scope.   3. What are the maximum, minimum and usual dimensions and individual weights?

34.titleEn: Choosing an Industrial Furnace Manufacturer in Jiangsu: Five Levels of Capability
34.summaryEn: Compare design, manufacturing, acceptance, delivery and after-sales support using the same project inputs and evidence.
34.contentEn:
A suitable furnace manufacturer can turn your operating requirements into a manufacturable design, verify it with agreed methods, deliver within defined responsibilities and provide practical support after production starts.

Versions of a Suneng gas-fired trolley-furnace quotation separately list quantities, prices and buyer-supplied items; some configuration quantities and prices change between versions. Attach each supplier response to its supporting document and version, distinguishing confirmed inclusions, confirmed exclusions and information still required. Missing information is not proof of missing capability, but an unresolved scope cannot be compared directly by total price with an explicitly included scope.

Compare five levels: design, manufacturing, acceptance, delivery and after-sales support. Factory size, certificates, promotional videos and prices are useful background, but none alone proves project fit. This framework is published by Suneng and applies equally to Suneng and every other candidate.

Why the requirement comes before the company name

Heavy-load trolley furnaces, carburizing multipurpose furnaces, vacuum furnaces, plate lines, aluminium solution/ageing lines, industrial kilns and old-furnace retrofits need different process, structural, control and acceptance capabilities.

Define material, shape, individual weight and loading; treatment, maximum/usual temperature and curve; load, cycle, shifts and annual capacity; energy, utilities, environmental and safety conditions; effective zone, uniformity, traceability and documents; and new/retrofit scope, location, shutdown and responsibilities. Different requirements cannot share one universal “best supplier.”

1. Design capability

Look at the questions a supplier asks. A useful assessment requests drawings, material, loading, curves, output, energy, layout and acceptance, and identifies assumptions and unknowns. Chamber dimensions alone do not determine load capacity, heating, zones, circulation, seals and controls.

EvidenceWhat to check
Requirement confirmationWorkpiece, loading, process, output, energy, controls, acceptance and site.
Loading/general arrangementWorkpieces, fixtures, effective zone, handling and maintenance space.
Key calculation summaryInputs and boundaries for loading, thermal input/power, circulation and cycle.
Control descriptionZones, recipes, records, alarms, interlocks and interfaces matched to the process.
Draft acceptance planHow key performance will be verified, identified before the quotation.

Complete proprietary designs need not be public, but appropriate summaries and lists should be available under confidentiality arrangements.

2. Manufacturing capability

Trace the design into the actual equipment through material and dimensional checks on the body, trolley, door and conveyors; lining layers, anchors, expansion joints and critical installation records; heating or burner layout, zones and interlocks; fans, flow guides, seals and exhaust; cabinets, wiring, sensors, instruments and program versions; and no-load trials, alarms, records and resolution of factory issues.

For critical projects, agree witness points at design freeze, material receipt, completed lining, electrical energisation, no-load trials and factory acceptance. State what will be witnessed, notice periods and handling of nonconformities.

3. Acceptance capability

“Meets national standards” is incomplete unless the standard, contract and test conditions are connected. For uniformity, define the effective zone, temperatures, no-load or loaded state, point number and arrangement, stabilisation and recording intervals, instruments and sensors, evaluation, retests and documents.

A factory acceptance test checks the agreed pre-dispatch items. Measurement-system accuracy, integrated operation, capacity and process results after installation still require the contracted site acceptance or specific verification. Do not substitute one stage for another.

4. Delivery capability

Similar furnace bodies can have different total prices because responsibilities differ. Compare packaging, transport, insurance, unloading and lifting; foundations, rails, platforms, flues and site fabrication; electricity, gas, cooling water, compressed air and exhaust; primary and secondary cables, trays and earthing; installation, commissioning, trial production and training; spares, special tools, drawings, programs and documents; factory/site and third-party tests and corrective work; warranty start, delayed acceptance and change management.

Align inclusions and exclusions before comparing totals. A lower equipment price may simply leave more site and verification work to the buyer.

5. After-sales capability

Replace vague “lifetime service” wording with reporting channels during and outside working hours; initial response, remote diagnosis and site attendance arrangements; wear and critical spare parts, lead times and substitution rules; program, password and backup responsibilities; attribution of faults involving operation, maintenance, incoming material, utilities or environment; and in-warranty and out-of-warranty charges and scope.

A nearby address can help, but “local in Jiangsu” is not a service commitment. Put response methods and times in the contract.

Use one comparison table

LevelQuestionEvidenceConcern

ManufacturingWhich stages can be witnessed?Plan, inspection points and sample records.Finished photographs without process records.
AcceptanceWhat is measured, where and against what?Factory/site plans, point maps, instruments and records.An isolated performance number.
DeliveryWhat does the total include and exclude?Supply list, responsibility matrix and schedule.Unclear interfaces and extra work.
SupportWho does what after a fault, and when?Service process, spares and contract terms.Only “prompt” or “lifetime” claims.

This is not a mechanical scoring exercise. Weight evidence according to project risks such as carburizing atmosphere, heavy trolley loads, continuous-line cycle or low-nitrogen-oxide emissions.

When to investigate further

  • Universal price, energy, uniformity or savings promises without workpiece and curve inputs.
  • A certificate used in place of furnace, process and project evidence.
  • Customer names without scope, timing or verifiable material.
  • Equipment names without configuration, interfaces and inclusions/exclusions.
  • “National standard” acceptance without the actual standard and method.
  • Fixed retrofit time or results without a site diagnosis.
  • Service slogans without reporting arrangements, spares and response terms.

This supports considering Suneng for corresponding custom furnaces, line equipment and existing-furnace modifications, not automatic suitability for every process. Its engineering team assesses workpieces, curves, loading, output, energy, acceptance and the site before proceeding. Confirm unlisted types and service boundaries in the project documents.

Suneng does not provide per-piece subcontract heat treatment or offer projects as an engineering, procurement and construction general contractor. Uniformity, savings, emissions, output, schedule and price conclusions require defined test or delivery conditions.

Common questions

Is a larger manufacturer always better?

Size indicates some resources but does not replace matching experience, technical evidence, quality records and a suitable team.

Do more certificates mean better equipment performance?

No. Certificates cover their stated systems or qualifications; equipment performance requires project-specific design, manufacturing and tests.

Can the lowest bidder be selected?

It can be considered after aligning operating conditions, configuration, supply, acceptance and support. Different inclusions make total prices incomparable.

Is a factory visit necessary?

For high-value, custom, continuous-line or higher-risk retrofit projects, consider a visit or remote/on-site witness points. Examine people, documents, work in progress and records, not only building size.

32.titleEn: What Parameters Are Needed for a Trolley Furnace Quotation?
32.summaryEn: Align eight groups of inputs, including workpieces, loading, process, output, energy, controls, acceptance and site responsibilities.
32.contentEn:
Sampled Suneng trolley-furnace proposals and quotations identify eight essential input groups: workpieces, loading, process, capacity, energy, controls, acceptance and site conditions. Chamber length, width and height alone cannot reliably determine trolley load capacity, heating, zones, interlocks, installation scope or final price.

A Suneng variable-capacity trolley-furnace proposal assigns support blocks and tooling to the buyer, with the buyer supplying product geometry and the seller providing the design. Provide workpiece and tooling weights, the support arrangement and site rail conditions, and ask the quotation to state whether blocks, rails and site works are included. A furnace name or workpiece dimensions alone can leave loading and site provisions unresolved until later.

An initial discussion is possible with incomplete information, but the resulting material must state assumptions, inclusions, exclusions and validity conditions. It is not a formal quotation for a frozen configuration. Similar chamber dimensions can lead to different structures, heating, controls and delivery scopes when weight, recipes, loading, energy, records or site boundaries differ.

The eight input groups

GroupInformation to supplyWhat it affects
1. WorkpieceName, grade, largest/smallest/usual dimensions, individual weight, drawing or photograph.Process suitability, effective zone, fixtures, support, surface quality and cleanliness.
2. LoadingPieces per batch, total load, layout, fixture weight, load distribution and lifting.Trolley, hearth, wheels, rails, drive and handling space.
3. ProcessMaximum and usual temperatures, full curve, cooling, atmosphere and surface requirements.Lining, heating, zones, circulation, doors and seals.
4. CapacityBatch cycle, shifts, working days, annual output and changeovers.Utilisation, power or thermal input, furnace quantity, production cycle and backup capacity.
5. EnergyElectrical capacity and voltage, gas pressure and flow, local restrictions.Heat source, distribution, combustion, exhaust and utility interfaces.
6. ControlsManual/automatic scope, recipes, records, export, networking, alarms and permissions.Controller or instruments, zones, recording, sensors and interlock logic.
7. AcceptanceEffective zone, uniformity conditions, test state, points, records, documents and third-party needs.Measurement, accuracy checks, test fixtures, acceptance and handover.
8. Site and project scopeNew/retrofit, building dimensions, foundations, rails, lifting, material flow, environmental conditions and installation window.Layout, transport sections, utilities, site work and buyer/seller responsibilities.

Always state units: for example, mm for dimensions, kg or t for weight, °C for temperature and pieces/year or t/year for output. The effective working zone is the agreed loading area in which process conditions can be met; it is normally smaller than the geometric chamber and must be checked with fixtures, clearances and heat circulation.

1. Workpieces: identify what will be processed

Provide the grade, shape, dimensions, weight and drawings showing support or clamping positions. These affect temperature, supports, surface quality, distortion and atmosphere as well as physical fit. For mixed products, include the smallest and most common specifications as well as the largest; designing only around the largest item may leave poor utilisation in routine production.

2. Loading: describe the arrangement as well as the weight

Individual weight, quantity, fixtures and total load affect the trolley frame, wheels, rails, drive and hearth. Load distribution, support points and stacking affect structural checks and available space.

Supply a loading sketch showing workpieces and fixtures. Workpiece dimensions are not the effective-zone dimensions: allow for loading, circulation, operation and maintenance. The project design determines clearances; this article does not prescribe a universal allowance.

3. Process: give the curve, not only the maximum temperature

State grade, treatment, maximum and usual temperatures, heating rate, holding time, cooling or unloading method and the required recipes. Rapid heating and slow heating with prolonged holding can require different heat input, lining thermal mass, zones and production cycles even at the same maximum temperature. “Trolley furnace” describes a structure, not a fixed treatment.

4. Capacity: calculate from the complete production cycle

Include loading, entry, heating, holding, cooling or exit, unloading and changeover. Supply shifts, working days, annual target, usual loading and allowable production variation. The batch cycle is the interval from loading to readiness for the next cycle.

A higher nominal load does not necessarily increase annual output if heating, handling or changeover is the bottleneck. Compare utilisation, furnace quantity and production organisation.

5. Energy: compare more than equipment prices

Suneng's sampled proposals include electric resistance and gas heating. Electric versions need supply, transformer and distribution checks. Gas versions additionally need the fuel type, pressure, flow, combustion safety, exhaust and site requirements.

Compare these against temperature, output, local utilities and delivery scope. Neither is inherently cheaper for every duty. Mark unconfirmed utility inputs explicitly and state the assumptions used.

6. Controls and traceability

Specify programmed temperature control, recipes, records, export, networking, permissions, fault alarms and remote interfaces. Define door, trolley and heating interlocks.

Zone counts, programmable control, paperless recording and movement interlocks vary between Suneng projects. Do not treat one instrument brand, zone count or interface as standard for every furnace. The agreed control description and electrical drawings govern delivery.

7. Acceptance requirements in the enquiry

For uniformity, state the effective zone, test temperatures, no-load or loaded state, measurement points, stabilisation time, records and evaluation method. A temperature-deviation number alone is incomplete.

Suneng can support contracted furnace-uniformity and control-system accuracy checks. Metrological calibration or third-party certification requires appropriately qualified organisations. A factory acceptance test does not establish that every condition after site installation has been met; define site acceptance separately.

8. Site conditions and delivery responsibilities

For a new project, provide the workshop plan, clear height, access route, foundations and rails, crane capacity, material-flow direction and utilities. For a retrofit, add drawings, photographs, faults, potentially retained components and the shutdown window. Suneng can undertake trolley-furnace retrofits; retained items and shutdown arrangements require site review and agreement.

Historical itemised quotations show that packaging, transport, commissioning, foundations, secondary cables, cable trays, lifting and utilities may sit outside the furnace body price. State the responsibility for each:

  • Systems included in the equipment.
  • Transport, unloading and lifting.
  • Foundations, rails, secondary cables and cable trays.
  • Water, electricity, gas and exhaust connection boundaries.
  • Installation, commissioning, training and acceptance.
  • Spares, documents, warranty and support.
  • Tax, freight and quotation validity conditions.

Starting an enquiry with incomplete information

Supply a minimum package: product name, material and drawing/photo; maximum dimensions, individual weight and total batch weight; maximum temperature and existing curve; shifts or annual output target; available energy; and whether the project is new or a retrofit and where it is located.

31.titleEn: What Is a Trolley Furnace, and Which Workpieces Does It Suit?
31.summaryEn: Compare loading, workpiece shape and weight, process, production cycle and site conditions before selecting a batch trolley furnace.
31.contentEn:
A trolley furnace normally combines a fixed furnace body with a movable hearth or trolley for batch loading, heating and unloading. The name describes its handling structure, not a particular heat treatment. It is often considered for large, heavy or irregular castings, forgings, welded structures, dies, machined parts and steel structures that benefit from loading a complete batch by overhead crane.

Suneng variable-volume trolley-furnace documents place the load on a trolley and use a movable rear wall to establish different effective heating lengths. Trolley-deck dimensions, physical chamber dimensions and the selected effective heating zone are therefore distinct. Mark the working area, workpieces and supports on the layout, then check the door and handling route. A workpiece fitting on the trolley does not establish that the complete heat-treatment task is suitable.

Size alone does not establish suitability. Confirm material, maximum dimensions, individual and total load weight, process and temperature curve, production cycle, rails and lifting conditions before defining the chamber, load capacity, heating method or price.

Main components

Workpieces are supported on the trolley, which travels along rails into the chamber. After the batch's heating and holding stages, the trolley withdraws for crane or other handling access.

Typical systems include the body and lining, door, trolley and drive, seals, resistance or gas heating, temperature controls, records and safety interlocks. Circulation, pressure control, exhaust heat recovery and automation vary with the workpiece, temperature and site. One project's configuration is not a universal specification.

Workpieces commonly considered

WorkpieceWhy consider a trolley furnace?What to confirm
Large castings and forgingsLarge dimensions or weight favour complete-batch handling.Envelope, individual weight, supports and heating/cooling curve.
Welded structuresWhole-piece stress relief or tempering of irregular shapes.Distortion risk, supports, effective zone and cooling.
Large dies and fixturesStable support and batch processing.Section size, clearances, uniformity and records.
Machined and steel structural partsMixed specifications and non-continuous batches.Pieces per batch, total load, process range and handling efficiency.
Shafts and rodsLong parts can be loaded horizontally on suitable fixtures.Length-to-diameter ratio, supports and distortion; compare a pit furnace where appropriate.
Mixed batch workRecipes can change between batches.Changeover frequency, recipe-change time, chamber utilisation and records.

A long shaft vulnerable to distortion on horizontal supports may suit a pit furnace if vertical lifting is available. Small, consistent parts in continuous high-volume production may suit a mesh-belt or other continuous line better. The chamber must also provide the necessary loading, heat-circulation and operating space around the workpiece.

Applicable treatments depend on the configuration

A trolley arrangement can be configured for batch annealing, tempering, normalizing, heating before quenching, ageing or stress relief.

  • Annealing: specify grade, heating and holding, cooling and supports.
  • Tempering: specify temperature, section size, load and uniformity.
  • Normalizing: define unloading and cooling as well as heating.
  • Heating before quenching: assess transfer time, cooling medium and interlocks together.
  • Ageing or stress relief: define the curve, holding, supports and records.

The furnace name does not make every material or treatment suitable. Maximum temperature, lining, heating power, zones, circulation and recording capability vary by project.

When to compare other furnace types

TypeHandling arrangementCommon application
TrolleyHorizontal rail travel and complete-batch crane handling.Large, heavy or irregular batch work.
BoxManual or mechanical loading through the door.Small and medium parts, small batches and trials.
PitVertical loading and lifting.Shafts or rods suited to vertical support.
Mesh beltContinuous conveying through the chamber.Consistent small parts suitable for belt transport.

Compare belt, roller-hearth or continuous lines for high-volume small parts; a pit furnace for vertically supported long work; and a box furnace for compact small-batch or development work. Special atmospheres, vacuum or narrow process windows require dedicated assessment of seals, materials and quality requirements. A site without adequate rails, foundations or lifting space also needs layout review before selecting a trolley furnace.

Eleven inputs for initial selection

  1. Product name and material grade.
  2. Maximum, minimum and usual workpiece dimensions.
  3. Individual weight, pieces per batch and total load.
  4. Clamping, stacking and lifting arrangements.
  5. Complete heating, holding and cooling requirements.
  6. Maximum design temperature and usual operating temperature.
  7. Uniformity, records and traceability requirements.
  8. Batch cycle, shifts and annual output.
  9. Available energy, electrical and gas conditions.
  10. Workshop space, rails and foundations, crane capacity and material-flow direction.
  11. Whether the project is new equipment, a retrofit or an overhaul.

These inputs determine more than chamber dimensions: they affect the trolley, doors, seals, lining, heating, zones, interlocks, foundations and installation scope.

Electric resistance or gas heating?

Suneng can assess either against the project conditions. Electric heating requires review of supply capacity, elements, zones and electricity costs. Gas heating also requires fuel pressure and flow, combustion interlocks, exhaust and local environmental requirements.

Neither is always cheaper to run. First align the workpieces, process and output, then compare configuration and operating costs using the local energy conditions.

Temperature uniformity needs defined conditions

Uniformity depends on the effective working zone, load, element or burner arrangement, lining, door seals, circulation, control zones and test method. Agree the target, measurement points, no-load or loaded state, stabilisation time and evaluation method in the technical agreement.

Suneng can perform contracted uniformity tests and control-system checks. Where third-party certification is required, use an appropriately qualified organisation.

About Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd.

Founded in 2006, Suneng designs, manufactures and integrates industrial furnaces and heat treatment equipment and provides installation, commissioning, retrofit and after-sales support. It does not provide per-piece subcontract heat treatment. Custom trolley proposals are assessed against workpieces, loading, curves, energy and site conditions. Confirm other furnace types and all parameters and delivery responsibilities in the project documents.

Common questions

Are trolley furnaces only for large parts?

No. Some medium parts with varied specifications and batch handling requirements may also suit them. Assess dimensions, weight, handling, process and cycle.

Can they process stainless steel or non-ferrous metals?

Confirm the grade, temperature, atmosphere, cooling, surface quality and contamination limits before selecting a standard, protective-atmosphere or alternative furnace.

What mainly distinguishes a trolley furnace from a box furnace?

The movable trolley facilitates heavy or crane-loaded work. A box furnace is generally more compact for small and medium parts, small batches and trials.

Can workpiece dimensions alone support a quotation?

No. Weight, load, curves, uniformity, energy, controls, foundations and installation scope are also required.

Can a uniformity figure be supplied in advance?

Only with the effective zone, loading and test conditions defined. There is no single figure for every trolley furnace.

Can an existing furnace be converted to a trolley furnace?

Assess its structure, foundations, rails, loading, heating, controls and interlocks first. A site inspection and technical review determine feasibility and retained items.

30.titleEn: Choosing an Industrial Furnace Retrofit Supplier in Jiangsu by Type of Work
30.summaryEn: Identify whether you need an overhaul, relining, heating, controls, energy improvements or relocation before assessing suppliers.
30.contentEn:
Before choosing an industrial furnace retrofit supplier, distinguish fault repair, complete overhaul, lining or heating renewal, control upgrades, energy improvements and relocation/restart. Ask candidates to identify inspection evidence, actual work, retained parts and verification for each affected system. These different capabilities cannot be reduced to “can repair furnaces”.

Suneng's trolley-furnace extension proposal connects mechanical changes, seals, heating and controls and requires testing of the modified furnace as a whole. Ask a retrofit candidate to state its responsibilities for those systems and interfaces, rather than simply whether it has worked on trolley furnaces. If it undertakes only part of the work, identify who handles the remaining design, installation and whole-furnace verification before comparing quotations.

1. Identify the type of retrofit first

  • Complete overhaul: restore reliability across ageing lining, heating, controls and mechanisms.
  • Relining: reduce structural heat loss and restore insulation.
  • Heating or combustion: restore or improve heat delivery.
  • Controls: stabilise execution of the process and provide records.
  • Energy retrofit: reduce overall energy consumption through justified measures.
  • Relocation or used-furnace remanufacturing: establish suitable, safe operation at a new site or for a new owner.

A supposed lining repair may actually need an overhaul; a controller replacement may have little effect when the main loss comes from poor insulation or seals. Diagnosis determines the appropriate scope.

2. Complete overhaul: look for system-level diagnosis

When: several systems have aged and faults are no longer isolated. Objective: decide what must change, what can remain and what is no longer worth repairing.

Check whether the supplier assesses site conditions and the remaining structure, reviews lining, heating, controls and mechanisms together, and connects design, construction, commissioning and acceptance. Common problems are charging for an overhaul while performing only local repairs, restoring an unsuitable structure and leaving scope unclear so that extra work accumulates. Interacting faults can recur when only one component is addressed.

3. Relining: materials and seals belong together

When: lining cracks, detaches or becomes friable, wall temperatures rise or holding consumes excessive energy. Objective: reduce heat loss and restore insulation.

Assess material selection against temperature, atmosphere and load, together with doors, openings and trolley-edge seals. Lining thickness must suit the furnace. Replacing refractory while leaving leaking doors unresolved, selecting unsuitable materials, or confusing a local patch with complete relining can undermine the result.

4. Heating and combustion: distinguish electric and gas systems

When: heating is slow, hot and cold areas appear, combustion is unstable or consumption is high. Objective: restore suitable heat delivery coordinated with control.

For electric furnaces, examine element condition, power and zone calculations, power regulation and thermocouple placement. For gas furnaces, examine burners, air-to-fuel control, ignition, flame supervision, gas interlocks and exhaust.

Replacing elements without checking zones and power may leave poor uniformity. Comparing fuel prices while ignoring ignition, flame and leakage safeguards is incomplete. New heating components must also remain compatible with the controls.

5. Controls: furnace knowledge matters

When: instruments are obsolete, programs are hard to maintain, curves cannot be stored, alarms are unclear or records cannot be traced. Objective: improve control stability, reduce operating errors and support traceability.

Review the controller, interface, instruments, zones, curves, alarms and interlocks. The logic must fit the process, zones, fans and heat source. A new cabinet cannot correct a temperature problem caused by lining, leakage, airflow or heater layout. A furnace specialist and automation team should assess the relevant interfaces together.

6. Energy retrofits: diagnose before choosing measures

When: overall energy consumption is excessive. Objective: identify the main losses and select individual or combined measures from the diagnosis.

Ask the supplier to evaluate lining, seals, heating or combustion, controls, fans, drives, recovery and operating practice against actual findings. Require consistent calculation and measurement boundaries. Energy quantity depends on furnace type, load, process and operation; financial savings additionally depend on energy prices. Compare corresponding operating data instead of accepting a fixed saving or payback. For waste-heat boilers, pressure vessels or other equipment within China’s special-equipment catalogue, verify the licensing requirements for the specific work and use providers holding the licences required for those activities.

7. Relocation and used furnaces: verify recommissioning capability

When: equipment is moved, restarted after inactivity or purchased second-hand. Objective: establish normal, safe operation under the new conditions.

Check the ability to reassess structure, lining, heating, controls, drives, interlocks, foundations and rails, then commission and run trials. Used equipment also needs a condition and feasibility review. A transport-only contractor may not identify process or control problems. Compare purchase plus remanufacturing with a new-equipment proposal, including uncertain history and possible concealed damage.

8. Quick comparison

WorkMain objectiveCapability to check
Complete overhaulRestore reliability.System diagnosis, remaining value and complete verification.
ReliningReduce heat loss.Material selection, seal condition and confirmed repair scope.
Heating or combustionRestore heat delivery.Electric/gas expertise, power and zones, safety.
ControlsStable process execution.Process knowledge and furnace/control integration.
Energy retrofitLower comparable consumption.Diagnosis, measures selected as needed and calculation boundaries.
Relocation or used equipmentSuitable operation.Condition assessment, recommissioning and trials.

9. Concerns common to every scope

Question quotations without operating information, single-trade work presented as a solution to all problems, unclear inclusions and exclusions, absent commissioning and acceptance, and fixed energy or payback promises unrelated to the site.

10. Suneng's retrofit scope

Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd., established in 2006 in Jiangyan, Taizhou, holds National High-Tech Enterprise certificate GR202432008987 and ISO 9001 certificate 03824Q60289R3S, valid until 11 January 2027, and has multiple Chinese patents. Its work covers furnace design and manufacturing, repair, retrofit, overhaul, energy improvements and site services.

Subject to condition and site assessment, the scope may include whole-furnace diagnosis and overhaul; lining and seals; heating and combustion; controllers, interfaces, zones and records; energy diagnosis and measures selected as needed; relocation, restart and remanufacturing. Suneng equipment and some other brands can be assessed. Imported equipment or incomplete documents increase uncertainty.

The referenced 2015 stainless-steel continuous annealing-and-pickling proposal sets out coordination of the annealing/solution section, combustion and controls; it does not establish completed site work or acceptance. It illustrates why a line cannot be assessed as an isolated furnace. The proposal and any project figures remain specific to the equipment, process, site and agreed acceptance conditions. Evaluate savings using comparable operating data.

11. Four practical steps

  1. Identify the intended type of work and objective.
  2. Prepare furnace dimensions, temperatures, material, load, problems, energy records, photographs and the shutdown window.
  3. Ask for the diagnosis, mandatory changes, retained items and risks, not only a statement that the work is possible.
  4. Compare aligned scopes and agree commissioning and acceptance in advance.

12. Common questions

How should a retrofit supplier be selected?

Match it to the work. Multi-system projects need coordinated assessment of thermal, mechanical, control and site requirements.

How does an overhaul differ from a repair?

A repair addresses a confirmed local problem; an overhaul restores several ageing systems. A local repair may leave system-level causes unresolved.

Will new controls fix high energy consumption?

They may improve stability and operating management, but cannot alone correct major insulation, sealing or heating deficiencies.

What makes an energy proposal credible?

A diagnosis, explicit measurement boundaries, coordinated measures and verification without unsupported fixed savings.

Is a used-furnace remanufacture economical?

Assess actual condition and feasibility, then compare total purchase and restoration costs with new equipment.

Which retrofit projects can Suneng assess?

Overhauls, relining, heating and combustion, controls, energy improvements, relocation, restart and used-furnace work requiring a coordinated equipment assessment.
