29.titleEn: Choosing a Heat Treatment Furnace Manufacturer in Jiangsu: Start with Your Process
29.summaryEn: Compare material-specific experience, heating and cooling interfaces, temperature verification and practical service capability.
29.contentEn:
A quotation based only on chamber dimensions does not establish process suitability. Add the material, treatment and acceptance conditions before comparing offers.

Suneng box-furnace documents provide separate records for furnace-control points and workpiece-monitoring points. When comparing heat-treatment suppliers, a furnace-temperature curve should prompt checks of the actual material, monitored workpiece positions, process sequence and product-inspection requirements. A record describes the process at its measurement points; it does not establish that a different material has achieved its annealing, normalising or other treatment objectives.

When selecting a heat treatment furnace manufacturer, check whether it can explain the relationship between this project’s material, treatment, loading, heating, cooling and acceptance. Then compare configuration and price. Heat treatment concerns material structure and properties; reaching the furnace setpoint alone does not prove that the workpiece meets its requirements.

When choosing a manufacturer in Jiangsu, the central question is whether it understands your treatment and material, rather than whose furnace is larger or cheaper.

1. Process understanding matters as well as manufacturing

Steel fabrication, electrical assembly and refractory installation are essential manufacturing skills. The harder task is making the equipment support the required process consistently. Annealing steel, copper, stainless steel and continuously moving strip requires different furnace arrangements, zones, atmospheres and speeds. Uniformity criteria and test conditions differ between ordinary structural parts and demanding precision work. Bright annealing requires appropriate atmosphere control and sealing; quenching requires coordination with cooling and transfer.

Look for questions about material, treatment and quality requirements before discussing chamber dimensions and price.

2. Match capability to the treatment

Annealing: confirm the material and annealing method, including whether the goal is softening, stress relief or structural adjustment. Steel, copper, aluminium and stainless steel need different temperatures and atmospheres. Bright annealing needs atmosphere and sealing checks; large workpieces need loading and holding checks; continuous strip needs zone length, speed, tension and cooling coordination.

Normalizing: this is principally used for structural adjustment of carbon and low-alloy steels, including a more uniform, refined structure. Do not describe all normalizing as softening or stress relief. Provide the material, incoming structure and required properties, then check the corresponding temperature and cooling cycle.

Quenching: assess heating together with transfer to the selected oil, water, polymer or gas cooling system, the cooling cycle and distortion control. Continuous lines also need coordination of conveying, quench equipment, lifting and washing.

Tempering: evaluate stable, uniform temperature, zone control, circulation and compatibility with the preceding operation's cycle.

Solution treatment and ageing: select the furnace and sequence for the alloy and treatment. Solution-temperature duty affects lining, heating and controls. Stainless-steel solution treatment requires the appropriate cooling route through relevant sensitization temperatures. A solution-treatment section within a continuous annealing-and-pickling line must be evaluated with the other process stages.

Continuous heat treatment: heating, cooling, conveying and controls must operate as one line. Zone lengths, speed, tension, cycle and upstream and downstream interfaces require coordinated design.

3. Process-to-capability checklist

ProcessCapability to examine
Steel annealing or normalizingZone calculations, holding uniformity and loading arrangement.
Copper, aluminium or stainless-steel annealingMaterial-specific experience and atmosphere requirements.
Bright annealing or controlled atmosphereAtmosphere control, seals and surface-quality conditions.
QuenchingHeating/cooling interfaces, transfer, cooling cycle and distortion control.
TemperingTemperature stability, uniformity and zone control.
Solution treatment or ageingProcess-specific lining and heating duty, cooling sequence and relevant material limits.
Continuous strip annealingZone length, speed, tension and cooling.
Continuous annealing-and-pickling or integrated lineLine cycle, interfaces and relevant line experience.

4. Five questions that reveal process capability

  1. Have you built furnaces for this material and treatment? Ask for a specific explanation rather than “we can do everything.”
  2. How will temperature uniformity be achieved and tested? Clarify no-load or loaded conditions, measurement points and the written criteria.
  3. Can process curves be recorded and traced to the required production records?
  4. How are heating, cooling and adjacent operations connected?
  5. What commissioning and acceptance will cover heating, loaded trials, control stability, interlocks, records and training?

5. Check the actual system when a furnace problem occurs

Uneven temperature can involve lining, heat-source layout, zones, circulation, thermocouples, seals, loading, workpiece weight and control logic. Rising energy use can involve aged insulation, leakage, heating efficiency, overshoot or operating practice. Quality variation can involve unstable control, distribution, missing process records or changed loading.

Present a real problem and see whether the supplier investigates the system before selecting replacement parts.

6. Service distance is useful, but not sufficient

For customers in Jiangsu, Shanghai, Zhejiang and Anhui, a nearby supplier can make surveys, installation, commissioning, maintenance and spare-parts coordination more convenient. Familiarity with local industries may also help. First establish process and furnace capability; proximity is an additional consideration rather than a substitute.

7. Proposals to question

Be cautious about quotations based only on dimensions, vague claims of experience with every material, uniformity figures without test conditions, fixed savings or payback without comparable data, heating-only proposals that omit critical cooling interfaces, and unspecified commissioning or acceptance.

8. Suneng's heat treatment experience

Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd. was founded in 2006 in Jiangyan, Taizhou. It holds National High-Tech Enterprise certificate GR202432008987 and ISO 9001 certificate 03824Q60289R3S, valid until 11 January 2027, and has multiple Chinese patents.

Subject to material, process and site assessment, its work includes furnace design and manufacturing for annealing, normalizing, tempering, quenching, solution treatment and ageing; trolley, box, pit, bell, mesh-belt, roller-hearth and pusher furnaces; continuous annealing, annealing-and-pickling and belt-line sections and line coordination; uniformity corrective work, controls and curve records; overhauls, relining, heating and combustion retrofits; and relocation, restart and remanufacturing assessments.

Suneng’s 2015 continuous annealing-and-pickling line proposal sets out coordinated changes to the annealing/solution section, combustion and controls. It supports the proposed scope, not completion or acceptance of site work. Such work requires coordinated assessment of the temperature path, cooling sections, relevant sensitization range and line cycle. The linked project page provides the specific context.

Equipment condition, process, site and acceptance objectives determine the actual proposal. Uniformity and energy results require stated operating and test conditions; project parameters cannot be applied universally.

9. Four steps to a shortlist

  1. Explain the treatment before asking for a price.
  2. Use the five process questions to examine capability.
  3. Ask for a system-level response to the real equipment problem.
  4. After establishing process fit, compare furnace experience and practical service coverage.

10. Common questions

Which Jiangsu heat treatment furnace manufacturer is best?

Choose for matching process experience and systematic assessment, not a general ranking or price alone.

How can process knowledge be tested?

Ask about your material, uniformity tests, records, heating/cooling interfaces and acceptance. Useful answers are specific.

How do selection criteria differ by treatment?

Annealing and normalizing require material-appropriate zones, holding and atmosphere; quenching requires cooling coordination; tempering requires stable uniform control; solution treatment requires suitable high-temperature and cooling arrangements; continuous lines require interface and cycle experience.

Who should investigate uneven temperature?

A supplier able to assess lining, heating, circulation, sensing, controls and loading together.

28.titleEn: Choosing an Industrial Furnace Supplier in Jiangsu: Five Provider Types and Selection Criteria
28.summaryEn: Match the provider to new equipment, local repairs, a full overhaul, controls or relocation, then compare scope and acceptance.
28.contentEn:
1. Match the supplier to the requirement, not a ranking

Shortlist Jiangsu industrial furnace suppliers for the actual task: new equipment, complete-line integration, repair or retrofit. Then check workpieces and process, supply interfaces and acceptance responsibility. Location can inform service arrangements; matching design and delivery evidence supports technical and quotation comparison.

Suneng mesh-belt line documents assign the wiring from the plant supply to the control cabinet separately from wiring between the cabinet and equipment interfaces. Such questions help distinguish responsibility for a component, an individual machine and a complete line. Ask each candidate where its work begins and ends, who supplies materials, who installs them and who coordinates commissioning. A nearby address cannot replace a clear project scope.

Clarify whether the project involves new equipment or an old-furnace retrofit; one furnace or a continuous line; relining or controls; a local repair or a full overhaul; energy improvements, relocation or used-equipment remanufacturing. Check whether the supplier understands the process and site and can define commissioning, acceptance and support.

2. Five common provider types

Jiangsu and the Yangtze River Delta have manufacturers and service providers for industrial furnaces, heat treatment, kilns and associated equipment. Their capabilities can be grouped broadly into the following five types.

3. The original equipment manufacturer

Suitable work: equipment still within the original manufacturer's service scope, replacement parts and local repairs, complete drawings and spare-parts information, limited structural or control changes, and continued use of the original design.

Capability to check: familiarity with the structure, original technical records, potentially better part matching and simpler communication for local repairs.

Limits: the original design may no longer suit changed processes, cycles or energy objectives. If the manufacturer no longer supports the type or cannot perform site modifications, consider a comprehensive furnace manufacturer or a specialist with a clearly defined scope.

4. A comprehensive industrial furnace manufacturer

These suppliers may combine design, manufacturing, installation, commissioning and retrofit capability. They assess structure, lining, heating or combustion, controls, drives, circulation, seals, site work and acceptance together.

Suitable work: new furnaces, complete overhauls, energy retrofits, combined relining and control upgrades, relocation and whole-equipment assessments of trolley, box, pit, bell, mesh-belt, roller-hearth and pusher furnaces.

Capability to check: whether the supplier can coordinate mechanical and thermal systems and organise the agreed integration and acceptance scope.

Limits: this may not be the lowest-cost route for a small refractory patch or simple cabinet repair. Its value is clearer where process stability, several systems, site work and acceptance must be managed together.

5. A lining or refractory contractor

Suitable work: local lining damage, aged insulation, chamber patches, furnace-door or opening repairs, masonry and fibre-module installation, especially where an approved design already exists.

Capability to check: whether mobilisation matches the shutdown window, and whether materials, labour and site costs are defined for the confirmed local repair scope.

Limits: refractory contractors do not necessarily diagnose the complete furnace. Unstable controls, ageing heaters, circulation faults, drive failures and poor door mechanisms may remain after relining.

6. An automation company

Suitable work: old control cabinets, controller or touch-screen upgrades, temperature instruments, process-curve recording, alarms, traceability, data acquisition and supervisory systems where the furnace-side requirements are already defined.

Capability to check: electrical expertise, programming, interface design, data records and coordinated controls within an agreed scope.

Limits: controls cannot be assessed independently of the process and structure. A new controller or instrument does not necessarily correct uneven temperature caused by the lining, seals, airflow or heater layout.

7. A relocation and maintenance provider

Suitable work: dismantling, transport, lifting, reinstallation, foundations and associated repairs for furnace or line relocation, used-equipment installation and restart projects.

Capability to check: experience with practical site construction and equipment movement.

Limits: furnace relocation also requires renewed checks of structure, lining, heating, controls, drives, rails and foundations, safety functions and trial operation. Moving and reconnecting the equipment is only part of the work.

8. Match the requirement to the provider

RequirementProvider to consider
New industrial or heat treatment furnaceComprehensive furnace manufacturer.
Local repair to existing equipmentOriginal manufacturer or comprehensive furnace manufacturer.
Local refractory repairLining or refractory contractor.
Complete overhaul or energy retrofitComprehensive furnace manufacturer.
Control upgradeFurnace manufacturer with an automation team.
Relocation and production restartFurnace manufacturer with a relocation contractor.
Used-furnace remanufacturingComprehensive furnace manufacturer.
Uneven temperature or a complex site retrofitStart with a comprehensive furnace assessment.

Specialists suit a confirmed local task. Projects spanning structure, lining, heating, controls, drives, construction and acceptance need coordinated responsibility.

9. Seven capability checks

  1. Furnace structure: type-specific inspection points for trolley, box, pit, mesh-belt, roller-hearth and pusher equipment.
  2. Lining and seals: cracks, distorted doors, opening leakage and continuous-furnace inlet and outlet losses.
  3. Heating or combustion: electric elements, zones and power; or burners, air-to-fuel control, ignition, flame supervision and interlocks.
  4. Controls and curves: controller, interface, instruments, zones, records, alarms and data export.
  5. Mechanisms: trolley, doors, belt, rollers, pusher, hood and fans.
  6. Site organisation: shutdown, lifting, access, utilities, construction boundaries and commissioning time.
  7. Acceptance: no-load heating, loaded trials, temperature stability, interlocks, records and a comparable energy-measurement basis.

10. Warning signs in a proposal

  • A low price without questions about furnace type, process, temperature, load or site conditions.
  • A single-trade provider promising to solve every thermal, electrical and mechanical problem.
  • Unclear inclusions, exclusions or items awaiting a site survey.
  • No commissioning and acceptance method.
  • Fixed energy-saving or payback promises without comparable operating data.

11. Where Suneng may fit

Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd., founded in 2006 in Jiangyan, Taizhou, is a National High-Tech Enterprise. It holds ISO 9001 certificate 03824Q60289R3S, valid until 11 January 2027, and has multiple Chinese patents. Its work covers industrial and heat treatment furnace design, manufacturing, repair, retrofit, overhaul, energy improvements and site services.

Relevant enquiries include custom new equipment; old-furnace overhauls; high energy consumption, aged lining or poor seals; coordinated assessments of structure, heating, controls and mechanisms; trolley, box, pit, bell, belt, roller or pusher retrofits; relocation, restart and used-furnace assessments; and projects requiring surveys, proposals, implementation and commissioning support.

12. A five-step selection process

  1. Define whether the project is new equipment, repair, overhaul, energy retrofit, controls or relocation.
  2. Prepare furnace size, temperature, material, load, problems, energy data, photographs and the shutdown window.
  3. Ask the supplier to explain likely causes, necessary checks and retained or changed components.
  4. Compare prices only for aligned work scopes.
  5. Agree heating and control tests, trials, interlocks, records and service responsibilities before work starts.

13. Common questions

Which Jiangsu furnace supplier is best?

Select for the project type and evidenced capability; there is no universal ranking across new equipment, refractory repairs, controls, overhauls and relocation.

How should a heat treatment furnace manufacturer be assessed?

Check furnace experience, process understanding, lining and heating, controls, site implementation and acceptance. Appearance and price alone are insufficient.

Should a retrofit go to the original manufacturer?

Consult it where support and records remain available. Changed duty or a system-level retrofit may justify an independent comprehensive assessment.

What matters for repair and retrofit work?

The ability to diagnose the interacting structure, lining, heating, controls, drives and site conditions, with clear responsibilities.

Are there furnace manufacturers in Taizhou?

Taizhou and the surrounding region have furnace and related-equipment businesses; Suneng is based in Jiangyan. Compare process fit, scope, site needs and service arrangements.

How can an energy-retrofit proposal be judged?

Look for site diagnosis, explicit calculation boundaries, coordinated measures and verification rather than unsupported fixed savings.

27.titleEn: Relocating, Restarting or Remanufacturing an Industrial Furnace: How to Assess Special Retrofit Projects
27.summaryEn: Establish the equipment condition before defining work on a relocated, idle or used furnace, or an individual mechanical or atmosphere system.
27.contentEn:
For relocation, restart after inactivity or used-furnace remanufacturing, check current condition and whether old records match the new site. Relocation requires interface checks; restart requires checks of changes during inactivity; used equipment also requires operating and repair history. Define retained, repaired, replaced and production-verification scope before comparing proposals and investment.

A Suneng solution-treatment furnace relocation proposal reuses the original fork mechanism while renewing controls, limits and parts of the hearth. At the new site, the tray supports, tine passages, rails and quench tank must be matched again. If the supplier says the original mechanism can be retained, request the old and new arrangements and the reassembly verification scope. Operating records from the original site do not by themselves establish readiness to restart at the new site.

1. Restoring heat treatment equipment after relocation

Treat dismantling, transport and reinstallation as one engineering project. Before dismantling, record installation, pipe connections, wiring and control parameters. During removal and transport, protect the structure, lining, mechanisms and electrical equipment and secure large components against distortion and impact. Reinstallation includes foundations, rails, alignment, mechanisms, wiring, control commissioning, heating trials and process verification.

Common problems include cracked or detached lining, distorted mechanisms, lost wiring references, missing parameter backups and changed temperature distribution. Record and back up the original condition, then perform complete checks and commissioning after reassembly. Relocation should be treated as a limited retrofit followed by renewed acceptance, not merely taking equipment apart and putting it back.

2. Restarting a furnace after years out of service

Do not energise an idle furnace simply to see whether it works. First assess damp, aged or friable lining; corroded steelwork; seized drives and ineffective lubrication; aged electrical components and reduced insulation; damaged or inaccurate controls and instruments; degraded seals; and, where fitted, gas piping, valves and safety devices.

Check structure and lining, mechanical operation, electrical insulation and safety, control availability, interlocks and the fuel system. Identify what can be reused, what needs repair or replacement and what must be addressed before operation. Long inactivity with little maintenance generally increases restoration work. Unassessed trial operation can create safety risks and further damage.

3. Remanufacturing a used heat treatment furnace

A used furnace may reduce equipment investment if its condition and suitability are established first. Confirm furnace type and size against the process, actual age and duty, structure, lining, mechanisms and controls, available drawings and programs, replacement-part availability and whether the modified furnace can meet the required process and output.

Possible work includes relining, mechanical repairs, controls, heating-system replacement, safety improvements and adaptation to the new process. Unclear history can hide damage, so uncertainty is often greater than with a familiar in-house furnace. Compare purchase plus remanufacturing costs with new equipment, not the used-furnace price alone.

4. Separate overhauls of mechanical or atmosphere systems

Pusher-furnace mechanisms

Long service can cause jams, wear and unstable movement in pushers, trays, guides and discharge interfaces. Work may include repairing or replacing the pusher, checking trays and guides, servicing drives and improving jam protection. Verify the production cycle and continuous operation after repair; no-load movement alone is insufficient.

Bell-furnace atmosphere systems

Protective-atmosphere systems involve gas supply, seals, flow control and safety. Upgrades may change seals, flow and control arrangements, interlocks and integration with the main controller. Assess sealing and safety carefully for the installed system.

A targeted overhaul can avoid unnecessary whole-furnace work, but only after establishing that the problem is concentrated in the selected system rather than caused by another part of the equipment.

5. Principles shared by these projects

  • Assess before modifying: establish condition before defining scope.
  • Check safety: investigate electrical, fuel, mechanical and structural concerns.
  • Record and back up: preserve installation references, programs and parameters.
  • Allow for uncertainty: reflect unresolved conditions in the proposal and budget.
  • Compare new equipment where appropriate: do not force a repair when condition or cost makes it unsuitable.

7. Common questions

How is production restored after a factory move?

Plan records and backups, dismantling, transport, reinstallation, commissioning and acceptance as a connected sequence. Reassembly does not automatically establish readiness.

Can a furnace idle for years be restarted?

It may be possible after assessment and necessary repairs. Check lining, corrosion, mechanisms, insulation, instruments and safety before energising it.

Is remanufacturing a used furnace economical?

Compare confirmed equipment condition and purchase plus restoration costs with new equipment, allowing for unknown history and hidden damage.

Can pusher mechanisms be overhauled separately?

Yes, if diagnosis confirms that scope is appropriate. Verify loaded, continuous operation at the required production cycle after the work.

How is a bell-furnace atmosphere system upgraded?

Assess gas supply, seals, flow, controls, interlocks and integration together, then define an equipment-specific safe implementation.

26.titleEn: Industrial Furnace Energy Retrofits: Insulation, Controls and Flue-Gas Heat Recovery
26.summaryEn: Review seven possible improvement areas against the furnace condition, production baseline and practical implementation limits.
26.contentEn:
Begin an energy retrofit with operating and energy records to locate losses, then select lining, sealing, heating, combustion, control or heat-recovery measures. Check changes to workpieces and output before comparing production, holding and stopped states. Without corresponding evidence, do not attribute increased use to one component.

Suneng high-temperature trolley-furnace documents distinguish furnace-wall fibre modules, a local fibre blanket at the heating-strip connection, load-bearing trolley bricks and hearth plates. First locate the suspected loss or damage, then check the materials, joints and seals at that position. If a quotation gives only a refractory grade, ask where it will be used, what area is covered and how the work will be checked. A material name cannot prove lower whole-furnace heat loss or energy consumption.

1. Lining and insulation

Assess refractory and insulation damage, heat loss, material suitability and the existing layered structure. Select materials and thickness for the furnace geometry, working temperature and process. Thicker insulation is not always the best solution: it must remain compatible with the equipment structure, usable space and thermal duty.

2. Doors, openings and seals

Investigate heat leakage at doors, observation openings, trolley interfaces, lids and other joints. Check alignment, compression and the mechanism as well as the sealing material. Soft, sand or water seals are applicable only where the furnace design and operating conditions support them. Reducing uncontrolled leakage requires a suitable complete arrangement.

3. Temperature controls and records

A programmable controller, operator interface, zoned temperature control, stored curves, alarms, interlocks and operating records can support more consistent operation. Sensors, control logic and actuators must work together. Reducing overshoot or unnecessary holding requires process-compatible settings and verification, not merely new hardware.

4. Electric heating or combustion

For electric furnaces, assess heating elements, circuits, power distribution and power control. For fuel-fired furnaces, review burners, air-to-fuel control, pressure, exhaust, ignition and safety functions. Converting between electricity and gas requires a separate assessment of tariffs, supply capacity, utilities, safety and economics. A change in energy source is not inherently an energy saving.

5. Fans, drives and heat circulation

Review circulation paths, airflow, fans and conveying systems against process requirements and the load. Variable-speed control may be suitable for certain operating phases, but reducing speed indiscriminately can affect heat transfer and uniformity. Identify restrictions, wear and loading effects before selecting a change.

6. Flue-gas heat recovery

Possible uses include preheating combustion air or workpieces and supplying another suitable heat demand. Assess flue-gas temperature and flow, operating hours, fuel, available space, fouling and the usable heat sink. Recovery equipment must fit the furnace and production schedule.

For heat-recovery equipment within China’s special-equipment catalogue, identify the applicable requirements by equipment category and activity. Design, manufacture, installation, modification or repair that legally requires a licence must be undertaken by a provider holding the relevant licence. They must not be included casually as ordinary furnace components.

7. Production and operating practice

Low loading, prolonged empty holding, incompatible mixed recipes, excessive door opening, poor loading layouts, inappropriate parameter changes and inadequate maintenance can increase unit-product energy. Review scheduling, loading and maintenance together with hardware measures. Preserve the required product quality and safety conditions.

8. When should other options be compared?

If the structure is badly deteriorated, the process no longer suits the furnace, energy-price changes undermine the economics, or implementation cannot fit the site and shutdown window, compare overhaul or replacement with the proposed retrofit. There is no universal investment-return period. Make assumptions, exclusions and constraints explicit.

9. How to set priorities

First collect equipment, workpiece, process, energy, output, fault and site information. Diagnose the dominant causes of loss, define mandatory repairs and optional improvements, estimate costs and benefits under comparable conditions, and agree implementation and acceptance. Verify the result using energy per unit of product and representative operating records rather than unmatched bills.

10. Suneng's service scope

Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd., established in 2006 in Jiangyan District, Taizhou, holds National High-Tech Enterprise certificate GR202432008987 and ISO 9001 certificate 03824Q60289R3S, valid until 11 January 2027, and has multiple Chinese patents. Its services include energy retrofits, overhauls, relining, controls, heating-system work and relocation/restart assessments.

Suneng can assess its own equipment and some furnaces from other manufacturers, subject to documents, component availability and site condition. Related service information and the three-line 1,250 mm stainless-steel retrofit provide project context. Final scope and results must be assessed for the particular furnace and operating conditions.

11. Common questions

What can an energy retrofit include?

Lining, seals, controls, heating or combustion, circulation and drives, heat recovery and operating improvements, as justified by diagnosis.

Where should high electricity consumption be investigated first?

Compare consumption with conforming output, load, temperature, cycle and operating hours, then examine the relevant heat losses and system behaviour.

Can relining solve the problem?

It can address insulation losses, but other causes may remain and require coordinated work.

Does a control upgrade save energy?

It may improve the execution of the process and reduce avoidable losses when sensing, logic and actuators are suitable. The actual effect requires verification.

How much energy will be saved?

That depends on the existing furnace, scope, process and operation. A fixed percentage without a baseline is not a reliable project estimate.

Should the old furnace be retrofitted or replaced?

Compare structure, process suitability, total investment, interruption, operating costs and future maintenance under the same requirements.

This article provides general guidance, not a project-specific performance guarantee. Agree the final technical scope and acceptance requirements for the actual equipment.

25.titleEn: What Information Is Needed Before a Heat Treatment Furnace Retrofit? An Assessment Checklist
25.summaryEn: Prepare eight groups of equipment, process, fault, energy and site information to make the initial assessment more useful.
25.contentEn:
Before discussing a heat treatment furnace retrofit, provide the nameplate and photographs, workpieces and process, current problems, operating and energy records, site layout and shutdown window. These establish equipment condition, possible reuse and production-recovery requirements. Mark missing information and arrange checks; do not invent values to complete an initial enquiry.

A Suneng solution-treatment furnace relocation proposal retains the loading fork but renews hearth supports, requiring the original trays and fork tines to be matched to the rails and quench-tank position at the new site. Alongside old-furnace photographs, provide tray and tine dimensions, the loading arrangement and the new layout. If only the nameplate is available, identify the missing drawings and arrange measurements; the old equipment name does not establish that reuse is feasible.

1. Basic equipment information

Provide furnace type and quantity, original manufacturer, service age, chamber dimensions, maximum and usual working temperatures, heating method, controls, drawings and earlier overhaul records. Identify furnace-specific structures such as trolley rails and doors, a pit lid and lifting arrangement, mesh-belt tensioning, pusher mechanisms or roller drives. Nominal dimensions alone do not describe their condition.

2. Workpieces and process

State material grade, dimensions, weight, load per batch or hour, loading arrangement, treatment, temperature and holding time, cooling route, atmosphere, required uniformity and process records. The retrofit must suit the actual workpiece and quality objectives.

3. Fault and operating history

Describe when each problem occurs, its frequency and production impact. Distinguish no-load from loaded operation, one zone from the whole furnace, heating from holding and a first fault from a repeated failure after repair. Supply alarm, maintenance, measurement and curve records where available.

4. Energy and production data

Prepare preferably 3–12 months of electricity or fuel consumption, output, shifts, unit-product energy, annual operating hours, interruptions and maintenance. Record tariff or fuel-price changes separately. Without the corresponding production and operating conditions, energy bills alone cannot establish the improvement potential.

5. Site conditions

Record workshop space, lifting and transport access, electrical capacity, gas, compressed air, exhaust, cooling water, foundations and rails. Identify restrictions on hot work, working at height, night work and phased construction. These conditions influence feasibility, scope and implementation cost.

6. Shutdown and production arrangements

State the allowed shutdown, order commitments, holiday windows, whether phased work is possible, and any standby capacity. Consider prefabrication, permitted night work and time for commissioning as well as physical installation. A short shutdown must be planned against the actual work.

7. Acceptance objectives

Agree no-load and loaded trials, temperature-uniformity requirements, data records, energy comparisons, safety functions, data export, operator training and any third-party verification. Where applicable, distinguish a temperature uniformity survey from a system accuracy test: the former assesses distribution in the working zone, while the latter checks the temperature-measurement system. Define conditions and criteria for each.

8. Photographs and existing documents

Provide overall views, the nameplate and clear photographs of damaged or suspect parts, along with drawings, control programs, manuals, previous technical agreements, modifications, maintenance and acceptance records. Images support preliminary assessment but cannot replace all measurements and inspections.

9. What if documents are missing?

List missing information honestly. A supplier may need a site survey, field measurement, component identification and program review. Distinguish confirmed facts from assumptions and unresolved items in the proposal. Do not present guessed values as equipment data.

10. Suneng's assessment scope

Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd. was founded in 2006 in Jiangyan District, Taizhou. It holds National High-Tech Enterprise certificate GR202432008987 and ISO 9001 certificate 03824Q60289R3S, valid until 11 January 2027, and has multiple Chinese patents.

Its services include overhauls, energy retrofits, relining, control upgrades, heating-system work and relocation/restart assessments. Documents and site condition determine whether and how an existing furnace, including some other-brand equipment, can be assessed. The related service and stainless-steel line retrofit references provide background; the final scope follows the project agreement.

11. One-page preparation checklist

Information groupWhat to prepare
EquipmentType, quantity, manufacturer, age, dimensions, temperatures, heating and controls.
ProcessMaterial, workpiece, load, layout, recipe, cooling, atmosphere and quality objectives.
ProblemsSymptoms, timing, frequency, affected conditions, records and previous repairs.
Energy and outputConsumption, output, shifts, hours, unit-product figures and price changes.
SiteSpace, lifting, transport, utilities, foundations, rails and construction restrictions.
ShutdownAvailable window, production commitments, phases, prefabrication and trial time.
AcceptanceTest scope and conditions, criteria, records, training and outside verification.
Images and documentsNameplate, overall and detail photographs, drawings, programs and history.

12. Common questions

Which documents should be prepared first?

Start with basic equipment data, photographs, the workpiece and process, current faults and the desired outcome. Add drawings and operating records as available.

Can a furnace be assessed without original drawings?

Yes, an initial assessment can be arranged, but field measurement and investigation may be needed and uncertainty must be stated.

Are chamber dimensions enough for a quotation?

No. Load, process, heat source, equipment condition, controls, site work and acceptance all affect the scope.

Why is a site survey needed?

It verifies actual condition, interfaces and construction constraints that documents and photographs may not reveal.

What does an assessment establish?

It identifies feasible options, retained and changed items, missing information and the basis for a technical proposal and budget.

This checklist is general guidance. The final proposal requires review of the actual equipment and mutually agreed requirements.

24.titleEn: How Much Does a Heat Treatment Furnace Energy Retrofit Cost? Scope, Budget and Enquiry Inputs
24.summaryEn: Understand the seven main cost groups and compare quotations only after aligning the work, site conditions and acceptance objectives.
24.contentEn:
There is no fixed price for an energy retrofit of an old heat treatment, annealing, trolley, mesh-belt or roller-hearth furnace or continuous line. This is an equipment-specific technical and implementation service rather than a standard spare-part purchase. Local relining, seal repair or a control upgrade has a different budget from a complete overhaul involving combustion, heat recovery, drives and line integration.

Different quotation versions for the same Suneng gas-fired trolley furnace include changes to burner, sealing and electrical-control configurations, as well as price changes for some items of unchanged specification. A budget difference cannot therefore be attributed entirely to added or removed equipment. Separate quantity and specification changes, inclusion changes and unit-price changes before totaling equipment, site work and verification costs. Energy savings require a separate comparison under equivalent operating conditions.

First establish the main problem, what must change, what can remain, the acceptance objectives, the shutdown window, the basis for energy calculations and the quotation's inclusions and exclusions.

1. Seven common quotation components

  1. Site diagnosis and design: surveys, tests, measurements, drawing and operating-data reviews, decisions on retained and replaced components, and the acceptance approach.
  2. Structure and lining: chamber size, operating temperature, insulation materials and layers, removal, installation difficulty and any shell repairs. A small box furnace and a large trolley or continuous furnace involve very different work quantities.
  3. Heating or combustion: electric elements, zone distribution, power calculation and control circuits; or burners, air-to-fuel control, ignition, flame supervision, gas interlocks, fans and pipework. Changing from electricity to gas or vice versa also requires an assessment of utilities, safety, capacity and operating cost.
  4. Controls: controller, operator interface, instruments, thermocouples, zone control, alarms, records, stored recipes, cabinet work and system interfaces. Program development, logic and commissioning matter as well as hardware quantities.
  5. Mechanisms and auxiliaries: for example, trolley rails and doors, mesh-belt drives and tensioning or pusher mechanisms. Relining and controls alone cannot eliminate severe mechanical deterioration.
  6. Flue-gas heat recovery and related measures: assess combustion-air or workpiece preheating and exhaust improvements where suitable. For waste-heat boilers and pressure vessels, define the equipment, interfaces and responsible parties, then confirm the specific requirements applicable to that scope before including it in the budget.
  7. Installation, commissioning and production coordination: removal, erection, wiring, lifting, insulation work, trials, training and acceptance support. Site access, shutdown coordination and commissioning time may dominate implementation difficulty.

2. What changes the budget most?

Furnace type: box, trolley, pit, mesh-belt, roller-hearth, pusher and annealing/solution-treatment lines differ structurally. Continuous lines also involve upstream and downstream operations, conveying, cooling, tension, zone lengths and coordinated controls.

Work depth: fault repair, a system upgrade, a complete overhaul, a comprehensive energy retrofit and relocation/restart are different scopes.

Existing condition: age, faults and missing drawings increase diagnostic and construction uncertainty; undocumented equipment may require field measurement.

Process requirements: defined temperature uniformity, data records, protective atmosphere and energy targets require more detailed design and verification.

Site and shutdown: workshop space, lifting, removal, utilities and allowed interruption affect costs. Shorter shutdowns may require prefabrication or phased implementation.

3. Why chamber dimensions are not enough

Also specify the material, load, working temperature, heating and holding times, uniformity requirements, heating method, lining, door arrangement, controls, safety interlocks and site conditions. Two similarly sized furnaces used for ordinary tempering and prolonged high-temperature holding may need substantially different configurations. Chamber size supports an initial discussion, not a final price.

4. Overhaul costs versus energy-retrofit costs

An overhaul mainly restores reliability by repairing aged lining, poor seals, worn mechanisms, obsolete controls or failed safety functions. An energy retrofit aims to reduce heat loss or improve heating, temperature control and heat utilisation. Projects may combine both, but quotations should separate necessary restoration from optional energy improvements so that comparisons remain meaningful.

5. Energy savings and payback

Collect pre-retrofit energy data alongside output, shifts, process temperature and load; calculate energy per unit of product; estimate the proposed changes; include electricity or fuel prices; compare investment with expected savings; and plan verification over a representative continuous operating period.

Existing condition, production load, process, operating practice, prices, output changes and maintenance all affect the calculation. Payback is a model with explicit assumptions and boundaries, not a fixed promise. The linked 2015 continuous annealing-and-pickling proposal illustrates the proposed retrofit scope and the conditions behind its energy calculations; it does not establish actual acceptance.

6. Information to prepare for an enquiry

  • Equipment: type, photographs, chamber size, working temperature, heat source, controls, service age, drawings or technical agreement.
  • Process and production: material, workpiece size and weight, load, recipes, heating and holding requirements, cycle, annual operating hours and shutdown window.
  • Current problems: high energy consumption, uneven or slow heating, damaged lining, leaking doors, control faults, unstable mechanisms or frequent repairs.
  • Operating data: electricity or gas consumption, output, shifts, process temperatures, unit-product energy and recent maintenance records.

Budget accuracy depends on the completeness of real equipment and operating information.

7. How to judge a quotation

Check that it states the work scope, main materials and equipment, retained and replaced parts, schedule, commissioning and acceptance, controls, site work, training, exclusions, acceptance boundaries and subsequent support. A low total may cover only a local repair and exclude controls, installation and commissioning. Compare prices for the same scope.

8. Suneng's assessment support

Founded in 2006 and based in Jiangyan District, Taizhou, Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd. holds National High-Tech Enterprise certificate GR202432008987 and ISO 9001 certificate 03824Q60289R3S, valid until 11 January 2027, and has multiple Chinese patents. Its scope includes overhauls, energy retrofits, relining, control upgrades, heating-system maintenance and relocation/restart assessments.

Budget evaluation considers whether overhaul remains appropriate, mandatory and retained parts, control upgrades, energy-improvement opportunities, phased work, acceptance and the boundaries used for costing. Some other-brand furnaces can be assessed from documents and site condition. The Taizhou location supports coordination in Jiangsu and nearby areas. Final work and pricing follow the mutually agreed technical proposal and contract.

9. Common questions

How much does an energy retrofit cost?

There is no standard price. Provide the furnace, load, temperature, heating, lining, controls, mechanisms and site information, together with operating data, for assessment.

What is normally included?

Possible items include structure and lining, heating or combustion, controls, mechanisms, installation, commissioning and acceptance support. The quotation and technical proposal determine the actual inclusions.

How should an overhaul be estimated?

Separate lining, heating, electrical controls, mechanisms, site work and verification, then assess each against equipment condition and objectives. Dimensions or age alone are insufficient.

How should an old-furnace retrofit budget be prepared?

Define objectives and scope, separate mandatory and optional changes, assess process and site conditions and allow for identified uncertainties.

How long is the payback period?

Calculate it from investment, comparable unit-product energy, output, energy prices and operating regime. Do not assume one period applies to every project.

23.titleEn: Industrial Furnace Retrofit Acceptance: Temperature Uniformity, Energy and Controls
23.summaryEn: Define test conditions, compare like-for-like operating data and verify mechanisms, interlocks and records before handover.
23.contentEn:
Retrofit acceptance should check sealing, temperature and measurement, control records, mechanical actions, safety interlocks and loaded operation under agreed conditions. Energy projects also need consistent energy-metering and conforming-output boundaries. Set the test items, methods and pass criteria in the technical agreement before implementation.

Suneng trolley-furnace extension documents require the modified furnace to be tested as a whole, rather than testing only the added section. If the supplier provides records for a new cabinet or section alone, include the original equipment, new equipment and their connections in the acceptance scope. Confirm that the final working zone, measurement points and control records cover the modified furnace. An old report does not automatically represent the changed configuration.

1. Furnace structure, lining and sealing

Check the repaired structure, lining and insulation, doors and observation openings, and the seals at the trolley, lid, hood or hearth as applicable. Review material selection, thickness, installation quality and external surface temperature rise under the agreed conditions. These checks help identify heat losses and unresolved structural problems.

2. Heating, holding and temperature uniformity

Record no-load and representative loaded heating and holding behaviour, zone fluctuations, temperature uniformity and agreement between measurement, display and recorded data. Specify the effective working zone, test temperatures, load, measurement points, instruments and acceptance limits.

Where required, arrange a temperature uniformity survey (TUS) and a system accuracy test (SAT). A uniformity survey assesses temperature distribution across the defined zone; a system accuracy test checks the temperature-measurement system. They answer different questions and must not be substituted for one another. SAT in this pyrometry context means System Accuracy Test, not Site Acceptance Test. Retain the corresponding curves and test records.

3. Control-system stability and data

Where control functions change, verify the control system and its records separately. Check the programmable logic controller (PLC, which controls equipment actions according to programmed logic), operator interface, zone control, alarms, curve storage, export and permissions. Verify manual and automatic modes and their safety constraints. A new cabinet is insufficient evidence without functional tests and records.

4. Mechanical and conveying systems

  • Trolley furnaces: rails, trolley travel, furnace doors and seals.
  • Pit furnaces: lid movement, lifting and associated positioning.
  • Mesh-belt furnaces: tracking, tension and conveying under the agreed load.
  • Pusher furnaces: pusher action, trays, travel and jam handling.
  • Roller-hearth furnaces: drives, synchronisation, roller material and maintenance access.
  • Bell furnaces: hood, base, seals and atmosphere interfaces.

Arrange no-load, loaded and continuous operation appropriate to the equipment. Verify fault response and interlocks using agreed safe test procedures and include the results in handover.

5. Safety functions

Check the applicable overtemperature, fan, door-position, heating-circuit, emergency-stop and limit interlocks. For fuel-fired equipment, the project may also require checks of ignition, flame supervision, leakage alarms, purge, ventilation and fuel pressure. Atmosphere, furnace pressure, cooling and power-loss responses depend on the installed system. Testing must follow the agreed professional procedures for that equipment; this list is not an operating sequence.

6. Energy comparisons

Establish a baseline with the material, process, load, output, shifts and operating regime. Compare energy per unit of product over representative, consistent operating periods. Changes in production, loading, schedules or operating practice can invalidate a simple before-and-after comparison. Keep energy quantities separate from tariffs: lower fuel expenditure caused by a price change is not the same as lower energy consumption.

7. Why acceptance can fail

When acceptance does not meet expectations, review diagnosis, acceptance criteria, any unresolved system problems, shutdown and commissioning time, and the assessed capability of the retained structure. Resolve these uncertainties when defining the work rather than only at final handover.

8. If temperature remains uneven

Review lining condition, heating-element or burner distribution, circulation, thermocouples, control zones, doors and other seals, and the loading arrangement. Confirm the actual load and measurement method. A control setting alone cannot correct every heat-transfer or structural problem.

9. Suneng's retrofit support

Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd., founded in 2006 in Jiangyan District, Taizhou, holds National High-Tech Enterprise certificate GR202432008987 and ISO 9001 certificate 03824Q60289R3S, valid until 11 January 2027, and has multiple Chinese patents.

Assessment and implementation may include overhauls, energy retrofits, relining, controls, temperature-uniformity corrective work, curve records, energy evaluation and commissioning. Suneng's own equipment and some other-brand furnaces can be assessed subject to drawings, controls, components and actual condition. The linked service page and three-line 1,250 mm stainless-steel retrofit reference provide context; the scope and acceptance criteria remain project-specific.

10. Common questions

What should retrofit acceptance cover?

The agreed structure, lining, seals, heating, temperature performance, controls, mechanisms, safety functions, records, energy comparison and handover scope.

What if the temperature is still uneven?

Check the defined test conditions and investigate heating, lining, circulation, sensing, controls, seals and loading together.

Are electricity or gas bills enough to prove savings?

No. Bills must be reconciled with production, process, load, operating time, metering boundaries and prices.

How long does a furnace retrofit take?

The furnace type and size, retrofit scope, shutdown window, component lead times, installation and commissioning requirements determine the schedule. Agree the work and trial-run plan after reviewing the actual equipment.

Why might a retrofit fail to meet expectations?

Check whether the initial diagnosis was complete, the scope and acceptance criteria were clear, retained equipment constraints were assessed, and installation and commissioning time was sufficient. Establish the cause from project records before deciding on corrective work.

This is general retrofit-acceptance guidance. Use the technical agreement and applicable project requirements for the actual equipment.

22.titleEn: Choosing a Heat Treatment Furnace Overhaul Supplier: Structure, Controls and Service
22.summaryEn: Assess the complete furnace, define what is retained or replaced, and agree on testing and support before comparing quotations.
22.contentEn:
Frequent faults, uneven temperature, deteriorated lining, unreliable controls and rising energy consumption may require a systematic overhaul. Replacing a damaged part alone does not necessarily address the cause. Choosing a supplier means checking its ability to diagnose, implement and verify work on the complete heat treatment furnace.

Suneng box-furnace documents separate empty-furnace commissioning, loaded heat-up commissioning and acceptance against the technical agreement. Ask an overhaul supplier which level its work affects and what records it will provide. If the answer is only that the equipment starts normally, ask how the agreed load and actual process will be verified. Equipment-function checks, measurement reports and product inspections serve different purposes.

1. Look for understanding of the whole furnace

The assessment should cover the furnace structure; refractory and insulation; electric heating or combustion; doors, trolley, rollers, mesh belt or pusher; circulation fans; electrical controls; alarms and operating records. For example, uneven temperature may involve heating-zone layout, lining damage, circulation, sensors, seals or loading. A supplier should explain how these systems interact.

2. Require a site assessment before a firm proposal

Inspect distortion, corrosion and cracks in the structure, the lining, doors and seals, heating components, electrical condition and recurring faults. Review process requirements, energy records and the available shutdown window. The proposal should identify what will be retained, repaired, replaced or upgraded, what it is expected to achieve, its limitations and the acceptance criteria. A quotation based only on a few photographs leaves substantial uncertainty.

3. Compare overhaul, retrofit and replacement

An overhaul aims to restore reliability; a retrofit changes systems to meet a defined objective; replacement introduces new equipment. The choice depends on the remaining structure, process suitability, foundations, rails, mechanisms, controls, total cost, interruption to production and future needs. A supplier should help compare these options rather than assume every old furnace should be overhauled.

4. Define acceptance before work starts

Plan no-load and representative loaded trials. Depending on the scope, check temperature-control stability, temperature uniformity, sealing, mechanical operation, alarms and interlocks, recorded curves, operator training and handover documents. Agree the effective working zone, measurement conditions and criteria. Compare energy performance under equivalent workpiece, process, load and operating conditions; a successful start-up is not the whole acceptance procedure.

5. Assess controls and records together

Review the programmable controller, operator interface, temperature zones, sensors, alarm functions and records. Specify what can be stored or exported and which production or management interfaces are required. Replacing the screen or controller does not by itself create complete process traceability: the program, instruments, records and operating procedures must support the intended use.

6. Check experience with other brands and demanding sectors

Imported or unfamiliar equipment may require drawing recovery, field measurement, program review and identification of available replacement parts. Capability should be established for the actual equipment rather than promised for every brand.

For sector-specific or customer requirements, distinguish the document and assessment object. AMS2750 covers pyrometry for metallic-material thermal-processing equipment. Nadcap is an accreditation program for critical processes, including heat treatment. CQI-9 assesses automotive heat-treatment systems. They are not interchangeable supplier qualifications. Check equipment requirements, the process operator, testing party and exact assessment scope against this project; serving a sector does not itself establish accreditation.

7. Eight questions to ask a candidate supplier

  1. Will it investigate the site and explain the causes of the problems?
  2. Will it compare overhaul with new equipment where appropriate?
  3. Can it assess structure, heating, mechanisms and controls together?
  4. Will it list what is retained, repaired and replaced?
  5. Are the acceptance conditions written down?
  6. What control functions and operating records will be delivered?
  7. What relevant furnace and process experience can it demonstrate?
  8. How will spare parts and subsequent service be provided?

8. Suneng's assessment and service scope

Founded in 2006, Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd. is based in Jiangyan District, Taizhou, Jiangsu. 9. Common questions

What information should be supplied first?

Provide the furnace type, dimensions, operating temperature, workpieces and load, faults, drawings or photographs, energy and maintenance records, process requirements and available shutdown window.

Is an overhaul always cheaper than replacement?

No. Compare the complete scope, remaining condition, process limitations, interruption, operating costs and future maintenance. Extensive work on an unsuitable structure may not be economical.

Can only the controls be upgraded?

That may be feasible if the underlying heating, mechanics and measurement systems remain suitable. Confirm interfaces and acceptance requirements before defining a controls-only scope.

21.titleEn: Repair, Retrofit or Replace an Old Heat Treatment Furnace? Decision Table and Checklist
21.summaryEn: Compare equipment condition, process suitability, work scope and total investment before deciding how to proceed.
21.contentEn:
Start with structure and safety, process suitability, implementation scope and total investment when deciding whether to repair, retrofit or replace an old furnace. The fault location, equipment age or a single quotation is insufficient. Where information is incomplete, inspect the equipment before comparing executable proposals.

A Suneng solution-treatment furnace relocation proposal retains the original loading-fork mechanism while renewing its electrical controls and travel limits and changing the hearth supports. Reusing a mechanism does not mean retaining every control and interface. Ask the supplier to identify what will be retained, repaired, replaced and revalidated, then compare repair, retrofit and replacement on that common scope.

Distinguish repair, overhaul, system retrofit and replacement

Fault repair restores a function after identifying the fault. An overhaul restores several ageing systems within an assessed scope. A system retrofit changes the configuration to meet defined new requirements. Replacement selects a new furnace or line. There is no universal price ratio or age threshold separating these choices.

Use one decision table for the existing condition

Current conditionCheck nextComparison to make

Compare retrofit and replacement under the same conditions

Use the same material, workpieces, load, process, output, shifts and quality requirements. Include design, equipment, removal and installation, foundations, utilities, commissioning and acceptance, production interruption, operation, maintenance and future spares. Comparing furnace purchase prices alone misses site and production costs.

Separate advance design and material preparation from on-site removal, installation, dry-out, cold checks, no-load trials and representative loaded verification. A retrofit does not necessarily create a shorter shutdown; retained structures, work scope and site arrangements determine the result.

Define the work and acceptance conditions

  • Structure, lining and seals: investigate the cause of damage, supports and connections; specify what is retained and repaired.
  • Heating or combustion: define changes for the available heat source, load and control requirements. A change of energy source also requires utility, safety and emissions checks.
  • Circulation, conveying and electrical controls: check airflow or heat transfer, mechanism condition, measurement, actuators, interlocks, program records and recovery after shutdown.
  • Trials and acceptance: agree the effective working zone, representative workpieces, load, sensor points, instruments, records, observation period and criteria. Specify equipment functionality and workpiece quality separately.

Energy comparisons must identify materials, output, yield, operating time and the metering boundary before and after the work. Subtracting bills from different operating conditions does not establish retrofit savings. Put final requirements into the agreed technical documents.

Information for the first discussion

  • Equipment: type, nameplate, service age, chamber or effective-zone dimensions, overall and detail photographs.
  • Workpiece and process: grade, dimensions, weight, batch or hourly load, temperature curve, treatment and quality objectives.
  • Current problem: when faults occur, repair history, measurements and production records, and known safety concerns.
  • Site: energy, utilities, foundations, handling and maintenance access, and the allowable shutdown.
  • Available documents: drawings, programs, manuals, earlier modifications and acceptance records. Identify missing items honestly.

What do the project records explain?

The loading proposal for a 30-tonne bearing-steel-wire spheroidizing trolley furnace and the 75 kW trolley resistance-furnace proposal illustrate how loading, measurement and supply scope are documented. These proposal documents support the stated loading, measurement and supply scope; they do not establish delivery, acceptance or additional measured performance.

The 2015 continuous annealing-and-pickling proposal illustrates the planned fuel, exhaust-system and control scope, not completed work. The support-roller heat-treatment line illustrates the process interfaces of a new line. Projects with different workpieces and furnace types offer questions to check, not parameters, returns or delivery conclusions that can be copied to another project.

Next step

For a known fault or retrofit objective, review the service scope. For relocation or restart after an idle period, use the relocation and recommissioning guide. If the direction remains unclear, submit the available equipment information so the missing checks can be identified.

20.titleEn: Industrial Furnace Energy Retrofits: Combustion, Relining and Control Upgrades
20.summaryEn: Assess the whole furnace system, compare retrofit and replacement on equivalent conditions, and define measurable acceptance criteria.
20.contentEn:
To decide whether an industrial furnace energy retrofit is worthwhile, first confirm that the existing equipment can still meet workpiece, process and safety requirements. Compare retrofit and replacement using the complete scope: retained and renewed parts, site connections and verification before production resumes. Equipment age or one quotation alone cannot decide the outcome.

A Suneng trolley-furnace extension proposal includes not only a longer shell but also trolley wheels, rails, seals, additional heating and control integration, followed by performance testing of the modified furnace as a whole. Assess that connected scope against a new-furnace proposal for the same workpieces and process. If the retrofit quotation covers only the shell extension, add the remaining work and commissioning costs before deciding whether it is worthwhile.

The decision depends on structure, fuel, production load, insulation, controls, process and site. Where the main structure remains sound, assess a systematic retrofit alongside replacement. Compare investment, operation, maintenance, shutdown and production recovery over the same evaluation period before judging economics. Replacement may be more suitable where the shell, foundations, drives or process requirements have changed substantially.

This article outlines common retrofit directions, assessment, acceptance and risk controls.

1. Why does furnace energy use increase?

Increased consumption can arise from one abnormal condition or several systems. Match site findings with operating records before assigning a cause:

  1. Lining deterioration increases wall heat loss.
  2. Door or seal deformation allows heat to escape.
  3. Ageing combustion equipment gives poor air–fuel ratio control.
  4. Damaged or inadequate heating elements disrupt heating and the production cycle.
  5. Insufficient temperature-control accuracy permits overheating or fluctuations.
  6. Fans, drives and circulation systems run continuously at full output without variable-speed adjustment.
  7. High-temperature flue gas leaves without useful heat recovery.
  8. The production regime no longer matches the original design duty.

Assess the system before replacing a burner or a layer of lining. Select measures for the problems actually identified, checking separately whether combustion, insulation, controls, drives, flue-gas recovery and operating practice fall within this project.

2. What can an energy retrofit include?

Lining renewal and insulation

Assess lining renewal from the damaged locations, material condition and associated heat loss. Cracks, spalling, powdering and deformation can increase heat loss, slow heating and weaken insulation. Work may include removing old lining, repairing the supporting structure, selecting ceramic fibre, castable or brick for the duty, revising insulation layers and coordinating heaters or burners. Review actual structure and process suitability before defining the work.

Control-system upgrades

Check the actual condition and functions of relays, programmable controllers, temperature instruments and paper records. Age or recording medium alone does not prove inadequate measurement or alarms. Where traceability, export or remote diagnosis is required, check whether the existing system meets that need. Options include controllers, operator interfaces, zone control, curve recording, alarms and agreed data-system connections. Assess an upgrade when confirmed measurement, recording or control requirements are not met; temperature-field problems also require checks of heating, circulation, loading and seals.

Combustion-system changes

For gas-fired furnaces, combustion affects fuel consumption, temperature stability and emissions. Options include burners, air–fuel ratio control, zoned combustion, low-NOx techniques, fuel changes, interlocks and flame detection. By-product gas, lower-cost fuel or a stable gas supply may offer economic value. Assess calorific-value variation, pressure, safety controls and piping before judging a change by fuel price alone.

Flue-gas heat recovery

Some continuously operated furnaces, annealing furnaces, solution-treatment furnaces and heating furnaces can use flue gas to preheat workpieces or strip, preheat combustion air, supply a heat-recovery system or serve another process. Where the work includes a waste-heat boiler or pressure vessel, first define the equipment, interfaces and responsible parties, then confirm the specific requirements applicable to that project scope. The furnace supplier can coordinate furnace, combustion, heat-exchange interfaces and controls; every heat-recovery system should not be treated as part of the furnace body.

Fans and drives

Constant-speed fans, rollers, chains and pushers may lack load adjustment. Where duty varies, variable-speed changes, drive refurbishment and coordinated controls can reduce unnecessary consumption and improve stability. Assess the structure and production cycle; do not promise a saving percentage without operating conditions.

3. What should be assessed before a retrofit?

  1. Furnace type and design parameters.
  2. Age and current condition.
  3. Energy records for the preceding 6–12 months.
  4. Actual output and cycle.
  5. Process temperature and uniformity requirements.
  6. Lining, doors, seals and heating condition.
  7. Controls and electrical systems.
  8. Opportunities to use recovered flue-gas heat.
  9. Allowable production interruption.
  10. Budget and required payback period.

Pricing without these inputs can misrepresent the work. Survey the site first, then define the proposal, quantities of work, shutdown schedule and economic calculation.

4. Overhaul or replace?

Consider an overhaul or retrofit where the main structure, foundations and drives can be retained, the process remains fundamentally suitable, the cost is substantially below replacement, site space makes replacement difficult, or the issues concern energy use, temperature control, insulation or local deterioration.

Consider replacement where the shell, foundations or drives are seriously damaged; the furnace type no longer suits the process; capacity must increase substantially; temperature or atmosphere requirements have changed; retrofit cost approaches or exceeds replacement; or persistent safety problems remain. A usable structure and stable process justify assessing a retrofit; major changes to both call for caution.

5. What should acceptance cover?

Installation followed by successful heating is not complete acceptance. Depending on the agreed project scope, address empty-furnace heating, loaded trials, control accuracy, temperature-uniformity surveys, system accuracy tests, capacity and cycle verification, energy use per unit of product, emissions tests, alarms and interlocks, operator training and maintenance handover.

Record specific criteria in the contract or technical agreement. Compare energy consumption for equivalent workpieces, process, loading, conforming output and operating regimes, with a stated metering boundary. Evaluate economics separately using fuel prices and maintenance costs; a lower fuel price is not a reduction in energy quantity.

6. Project reference: three 1,250 mm stainless-steel lines

Suneng’s 2015 proposal for three 1,250 mm continuous annealing-and-pickling lines sets out fuel adaptation, fuel-gas and exhaust-system changes, solution-section changes and control updates. This is a proposed scope, not evidence of completed retrofit work or acceptance. Fuel-cost calculations in the proposal use assumptions about a particular year, prices and output. They must not be presented as measured energy savings or realized financial returns.

The figures apply to that project. Actual results depend on the original furnace structure, fuel, line load, insulation, controls, operating regime and site conditions and cannot be transferred to all retrofits. The existing project reference is available in Chinese.

7. What should a retrofit supplier demonstrate?

  1. Industrial-furnace design and manufacturing capability.
  2. Understanding of the structure, lining, combustion, electrical controls and mechanical systems.
  3. Site diagnosis rather than only a price for one replacement.
  4. A complete technical proposal.
  5. Relevant furnace or industry experience.
  6. A clear statement of included and excluded work.
  7. Explicit acceptance criteria.
  8. Long-term spare-parts and service support.

For custom furnaces, experience, defined technical scope and site diagnosis matter more than a low headline price.

8. Suneng retrofit services

Founded in 2006, Jiangsu Suneng Industrial Furnace Co., Ltd. manufactures industrial furnaces and provides energy-retrofit services. Its assessment scope can include energy retrofits, overhauls, relining, control and combustion upgrades, associated flue-gas heat recovery, relocation and restart assessment, and temperature-uniformity survey and system accuracy test work and corrective measures.

Suneng can assess its own equipment and some furnaces from other manufacturers. Imported or other-brand equipment requires a review of drawings, controls, spare parts and site condition. Existing service, company-profile and qualification pages provide further background.

9. Common questions

Will an energy retrofit always save money?

No. Results depend on the old furnace, fuel price, production load, work scope and operating regime. Begin with diagnosis and economic calculations.

How long will an overhaul stop production?

The label “local retrofit” or “complete overhaul” does not determine a duration. Separate design and procurement that can precede shutdown, dismantling and connections requiring shutdown, and commissioning and production validation. Schedule their dependencies against site conditions; local work may also depend on critical parts or interfaces.

Is a control upgrade necessary?

First investigate the causes and existing functions when temperature fluctuates excessively, records are incomplete, alarms are unclear or traceability is inadequate. Assess the upgrade scope after confirming that the existing system cannot meet the agreed requirements.

Can relining solve high energy consumption?

It can improve insulation. If combustion, controls, seals or operating practice also contribute, a wider retrofit is required.

Can equipment from another manufacturer be retrofitted?

It can be assessed against drawings, controls, available parts, condition and site duty. Suitability should not be promised without those checks.
